    only gets a cache discount on the tokens actually known to be cached.

1	"""Assign `price_score` to each candidate `ModelLLM` for one `Trajectory`.
2	
3	Per the README's scoring contract (§5): `price_score` is `[0, 1]`, higher = cheaper,
4	normalized *within this trajectory's candidate pool* — not against some global price
5	scale. This module is a pure function of `(Trajectory, List[ModelLLM])`; the only place
6	it reads `Trajectory.served_model` is the switching-cost check below, which the README
7	explicitly carves out as legitimate (it is not a task-quality proxy).
8	
9	The crux, per README §5: providers cache the shared input prefix across a trajectory's
10	calls, and a model switch resets that cache. So "cheaper per token" and "cheaper for
11	the next call" are different questions once a trajectory has accumulated context — a
12	model switch pays full uncached price for the whole accumulated prefix, which in long
13	trajectories can dwarf any per-token saving. That's the entire reason this module needs
14	`served_model` at all: to tell a HOLD's mostly-cached next call apart from a CHANGE's
15	fully-uncached one.
16	
17	`total_cached_tokens` is used directly as the already-cached share of that accumulated
18	context — see `_next_call_tokens` for why, and why an earlier version of this module
19	was wrong to instead assume the entire accumulated context was cached under HOLD.
20	"""
21	
22	from __future__ import annotations
23	
24	from data_models.model_llm import ModelLLM
25	from data_models.Trajectory import Trajectory
26	
27	
28	def _next_call_tokens(trajectory: Trajectory) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
29	    """ESTIMATE the shape of the trajectory's next call.
30	
31	    Returns (accumulated_context_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens).
32	
33	    `accumulated_context_tokens` is `Trajectory.total_tokens` taken at face value: the
34	    total input tokens billed across the trajectory's calls so far, before any cache
35	    discount (see that field's docstring). This is a *cumulative* total across every
36	    past call, not the size of any one prompt — a trajectory's calls each resend the
37	    whole history, so `total_tokens` is already the whole-trajectory-to-date footprint
38	    a switch has to re-pay. Treated this way, the "next call" estimate below reads as
39	    "the switch penalty at stake right now", which is what the cache trap is actually
40	    about, at the cost of overstating the literal byte size of one upcoming API call —
41	    see the README's "Known simplifications" for the size of that overstatement on long
42	    trajectories.
43	
44	    `total_cached_tokens` is a share of that same `total_tokens` (again, by its own
45	    docstring) — the part of it already known to be cache-eligible. An earlier version
46	    of this function computed `total_tokens - total_cached_tokens` and called *that* the
47	    "current context", then separately assumed the result was 100% cached under HOLD.
48	    That double-used `total_cached_tokens` in contradictory ways: first to define a
49	    quantity as "the not-yet-cached remainder", then to treat that same remainder as
50	    fully cached. This version keeps `total_tokens` and `total_cached_tokens` as the two
51	    numbers they actually are — a whole and its already-cached share — and never
52	    re-derives one from the other.
53	
54	    `increment_tokens` approximates how much *new* content (tool outputs, replies, ...)
55	    a typical call in this trajectory appends, as the trajectory's own average per-call
56	    growth (accumulated context / calls so far). There is no better signal available:
57	    the next call's actual new content is by definition not in the log yet.
58	    """
59	    accumulated_context_tokens = float(trajectory.total_tokens)
60	    increment_tokens = (
61	        accumulated_context_tokens / trajectory.total_calls if trajectory.total_calls else 0.0
62	    )
63	    next_output_tokens = trajectory.avg_output_tokens_per_call
64	    return accumulated_context_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens
65	
66	
67	def _next_call_cost(trajectory: Trajectory, model: ModelLLM) -> float | None:
68	    """ESTIMATE the USD cost of `model` serving this trajectory's next call.
69	
70	    Returns None if `model.context_window_size` can't hold the next call at all —
71	    that candidate is infeasible, not merely expensive, and is handled separately.
72	    Note the feasibility check compares against `accumulated_context_tokens` (the whole
73	    trajectory's cumulative footprint, per `_next_call_tokens`), which is stricter than
74	    the real constraint a context window enforces (the size of one actual prompt) — see
75	    the README's "Known simplifications".
76	    """
77	    accumulated_context_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens = _next_call_tokens(
78	        trajectory
79	    )
80	    next_input_tokens = accumulated_context_tokens + increment_tokens
81	
82	    if next_input_tokens + next_output_tokens > model.context_window_size:
83	        return None
84	
85	    holding = model.name == trajectory.served_model
86	    if holding:
87	        # Same model as the log: bill the trajectory's own already-cached share at the
88	        # cached rate, and everything else — the never-cached remainder of the
89	        # accumulated context, plus the new increment — at the normal rate.
90	        cached_tokens = min(float(trajectory.total_cached_tokens), accumulated_context_tokens)
91	        uncached_tokens = (accumulated_context_tokens - cached_tokens) + increment_tokens
92	    else:
93	        # A switch resets the provider's prefix cache: the whole next prompt is
94	        # uncached, not just the increment. This is the cache trap from README §5.
95	        cached_tokens = 0.0
96	        uncached_tokens = next_input_tokens
97	
98	    input_cost = (
99	        uncached_tokens * model.input_price_per_1m
100	        + cached_tokens * model.cached_input_price_per_1m
101	    ) / 1_000_000
102	    output_cost = next_output_tokens * model.output_price_per_1m / 1_000_000
103	    return input_cost + output_cost
104	
105	
106	def score_price(trajectory: Trajectory, models: list[ModelLLM]) -> list[ModelLLM]:
107	    """Enrich each `ModelLLM` in `models` with a `price_score` in `[0, 1]`.
108	
109	    Higher is cheaper. Costs are estimated per `_next_call_cost` and min-max
110	    normalized across `models` — this trajectory's candidate pool only, per README
111	    §5's "normalize within the candidate pool, not globally". Infeasible candidates
112	    (next call wouldn't fit their context window) are scored 0.0 and excluded from the
113	    min-max range so one unusable model doesn't compress everyone else's spread.
114	    """
115	    costs: dict[str, float | None] = {
116	        model.name: _next_call_cost(trajectory, model) for model in models
117	    }
118	
119	    feasible_costs = [cost for cost in costs.values() if cost is not None]
120	    if not feasible_costs:
121	        for model in models:
122	            model.price_score = 0.0
123	        return models
124	
125	    cheapest, priciest = min(feasible_costs), max(feasible_costs)
126	    spread = priciest - cheapest
127	
128	    for model in models:
129	        cost = costs[model.name]
130	        if cost is None:
131	            model.price_score = 0.0
132	        elif spread == 0:
133	            model.price_score = 1.0
134	        else:
135	            model.price_score = (priciest - cost) / spread
136	
137	    return models
138

258	## 5. Scoring
259	
260	> **Performance scoring is undefined as of this writing.** Price scoring is implemented — see
261	> "Price scoring formula" below. This section records the constraints any implementation must
262	> respect, not a design that has been agreed for the parts still open. When you settle one, write
263	> it here.
264	
265	### Shared contract
266	
267	- Both `price_score` and `performance_score` must be on the **same, comparable scale** —
268	  otherwise the weighted average in `model.py` is meaningless. Normalize to `[0, 1]`, higher is
269	  better (so cheap → high price score), and normalize *within the candidate pool for this
270	  trajectory*, not globally.
271	- Both are functions of `(Trajectory, ModelLLM)`. Neither may look at the `model` field of the
272	  trajectory it is scoring, except where the router deliberately reasons about switching cost —
273	  see the cache trap below. Leaking the served model into the score is how you accidentally
274	  build a classifier that predicts the log instead of a router that improves on it.
275	
276	### Price
277	
278	- **Token counts are estimates.** There is no `usage` field. The pipeline counts with
279	  **`tiktoken`, `o200k_base`, applied uniformly to every line of both families**
280	  (`trajectory_analyzer.count_tokens`); chars/4 remains only as a fallback when the vocab file is
281	  absent, so a machine with no network degrades instead of failing. Every number derived from
282	  either is an estimate and must be labeled as one in the writeup. Never present estimated tokens
283	  as measured.
284	  - *Why not chars/4:* measured against the real tokenizer on this export, chars/4 understates
285	    Claude text by 4% and GPT text by 9% — a 5-point **family-correlated** error, because
286	    tool-call JSON tokenizes at ~3.2 chars/token against ~4.15 for prose and the GPT lines are
287	    more tool-heavy. On a workload this tool-dominated it is wrong exactly where it matters.
288	  - *Why one tokenizer for both:* the ids are anonymized and map to no public tokenizer
289	    (`encoding_for_model("claude-opus-5")` raises), and Claude's tokenizer is not available
290	    offline. A per-family tokenizer would make the two families' prices incomparable — which is
291	    the only comparison the router makes. Uniform is the honest choice; it is still an estimate.
292	  - Cost: ~16 s for the full export, offline after a one-time 3.6 MB vocab fetch cached in
293	    `.tokenizer_cache/` (gitignored).
294	- **Tool schemas count.** All ~12 schemas are re-sent on every call — a median **4,203** est.
295	  tokens, and they sit at the very front of the prefix, so they are also the most cacheable part.
296	  `total_tokens` includes them.
297	- **Pricing is an assumption.** The model ids are anonymized, so no public price sheet applies
298	  and the tier order is not published. If the organizers post prices, they win; otherwise state
299	  the assumption explicitly and keep it in one place so it can be swapped.
300	- **The cache trap — this is the crux of the price model.** Providers cache the shared input
301	  prefix across a task's calls. A model switch **resets that cache**, so every call after a
302	  switch pays full price for the entire accumulated prefix. In trajectories this long, that
303	  penalty can dwarf the per-token saving that motivated the switch. A `CHANGE TO` decision that
304	  ignores this will look brilliant and be wrong.
305	  - Measured: **92.1% of all billed input across the export is cacheable prefix.** Total billed
306	    input is 338 M est. tokens; per trajectory the median is 116 K and the maximum **11.7 M** —
307	    cost is *quadratic* in trajectory length, because every call re-sends the whole history.
308	    Input dominates output ~130:1, so price here is almost entirely an input-side story.
309	  - No overlap search is required, and pretending otherwise would overstate what we know. Within
310	    a line, call *i*'s prompt is by construction a prefix-extension of call *i−1*'s, so under a
311	    perfect cache the cached share of call *i* is exactly call *i−1*'s whole prompt, and the sum
312	    collapses to `total_tokens − prompt_tokens[last]`. `Trajectory.total_cached_tokens` is that
313	    identity times **`trajectory_analyzer.CACHE_HIT_RATE`** (default `1.0`, the optimistic
314	    bound). Real caches have TTLs and minimum block sizes and the export has no timestamps, so
315	    that constant is the single place the assumption lives — sweep it from `price_model.py`.
316	
317	#### Price scoring formula (implemented, `router_models/price_model.py`)
318	
319	`score_price(trajectory, models)` estimates the USD cost of each candidate serving the
320	trajectory's **next call**, then min-max normalizes those costs into `price_score ∈ [0, 1]`
321	across the candidate pool for this trajectory (cheapest → `1.0`, priciest → `0.0`). It reads only
322	`Trajectory` fields plus one `ModelLLM` at a time — the only place it looks at
323	`trajectory.served_model` is the hold/switch cache check below, which is the exception the shared
324	contract above carves out.
325	
326	1. **Shape the next call, from `Trajectory` fields alone:**
327	   - `accumulated_context_tokens = total_tokens`, taken at face value — the total input tokens
328	     billed across the trajectory's calls so far, before any cache discount (per that field's own
329	     docstring). This is a **cumulative** total across every past call, not the size of any one
330	     prompt: each call resends the whole history, so `total_tokens` is already the
331	     whole-trajectory-to-date footprint a switch would have to re-pay. Reading it this way makes
332	     the "next call" estimate really mean "the switch penalty at stake right now" — see "Known
333	     simplifications" below for what that costs in literal prompt-size accuracy.
334	   - `already_cached_tokens = total_cached_tokens` — a *share of that same `total_tokens`*, per its
335	     own docstring: the part already known to be cache-eligible. Used directly, capped at
336	     `accumulated_context_tokens` for safety.
337	     - **This replaced an earlier, incorrect version of the formula.** That version computed
338	       `total_tokens − total_cached_tokens` and called the result "current context", then
339	       separately assumed the *entire* result was cached under HOLD — using `total_cached_tokens`
340	       once to define a quantity as "the not-yet-cached remainder" and then, contradictorily,
341	       treating that same remainder as fully cached. This version never re-derives one field from
342	       the other: `total_tokens` is the whole, `total_cached_tokens` is its already-cached share,
343	       full stop.
344	   - `increment_tokens = accumulated_context_tokens / total_calls` — an ESTIMATE of how much *new*
345	     content (tool outputs, replies, ...) a typical call in this trajectory appends, taken as the
346	     trajectory's own average per-call growth. The next call's actual new content is by
347	     definition not yet in the log, so this is the best available stand-in. (Unchanged from the
348	     original formula, modulo the renamed base quantity.)
349	   - `next_output_tokens = avg_output_tokens_per_call` (already excludes the trajectory's
350	     unobserved final output, per `Trajectory`'s own field contract).
351	2. **Feasibility gate.** If `next_input_tokens + next_output_tokens` (where
352	   `next_input_tokens = accumulated_context_tokens + increment_tokens`) exceeds a candidate's
353	   `context_window_size`, that candidate can't serve the call at all — its cost is `None`, it is
354	   forced to `price_score = 0.0`, and it is excluded from the min-max range so one unusable model
355	   doesn't compress everyone else's spread. Because `accumulated_context_tokens` is cumulative
356	   (see above), this gate is **stricter than the real constraint** a context window enforces (the
357	   size of one actual prompt, not the whole trajectory's resend history) — a long trajectory can
358	   trip it well before any single real call actually would. See "Known simplifications".
359	3. **Apply the cache trap to the remaining candidates:**
360	   - **HOLD** (`model.name == trajectory.served_model`): `already_cached_tokens` bills at
361	     `cached_input_price_per_1m`; everything else —
362	     `(accumulated_context_tokens − already_cached_tokens) + increment_tokens` — bills at
363	     `input_price_per_1m`.
364	   - **CHANGE** (any other candidate): the switch resets the provider's cache, so the *entire*
365	     `next_input_tokens` bills at `input_price_per_1m` — none of it is cached.
366	   - Either way, `next_output_tokens` bills at `output_price_per_1m`
367	     (`cached_output_price_per_1m` is 0.0 for every seeded model — see `pre_processing/model_list.py`
368	     — since neither pricing source discounts a freshly generated output token).
369	   - `cost = (uncached_tokens · input_price_per_1m + cached_tokens · cached_input_price_per_1m
370	     + next_output_tokens · output_price_per_1m) / 1e6`.
371	4. **Normalize:** `price_score = (max_cost − cost) / (max_cost − min_cost)` over feasible
372	   candidates; if every feasible candidate ties, all get `1.0`.
373	
374	This reproduces the cache trap directly: a candidate with identical per-token rates to
375	`served_model` scores strictly lower than holding, because a switch loses the cache discount on
376	`already_cached_tokens`; a much cheaper candidate can still outscore holding if its base rate is
377	low enough to absorb that reset penalty. With `total_cached_tokens = 0`, holding and switching to
378	an identically-priced model cost exactly the same — there is no cache to lose. Covered by
379	`tests/test_price_model.py` (full cache, partial cache, no cache, switching, and the feasibility
380	gate); verified against synthetic trajectories only, not yet against the real export (no chunk was
381	available locally when this was written — see §3).
382	
383	**Known simplifications, stated rather than hidden:**
384	- `accumulated_context_tokens` is `total_tokens`, a cumulative sum across every past call — not
385	  the byte size of one upcoming prompt. On the 20-call, 1M-token synthetic trajectory in
386	  `tests/test_price_model.py`, the real next prompt would be roughly 50K tokens; this formula
387	  prices the next call as if it sent the full 1M+, which is also why that same trajectory now
388	  trips the feasibility gate against a 1M-token context window even though the actual next call
389	  would fit comfortably. Accepted deliberately: it keeps `price_score` computable from `Trajectory`
390	  fields alone, with no re-derivation of `total_cached_tokens` into a different, inconsistent
391	  quantity — see the "This replaced an earlier, incorrect version" note above for why the
392	  alternative was worse.
393	- `increment_tokens` is a same-trajectory average, not a real prediction of the next call's size;
394	  a trajectory with unusually front-loaded or back-loaded growth will be mis-estimated.
395	- The formula scores one hypothetical next call, not the rest of the trajectory to come — it
396	  matches the README's "model for the next message" framing (§1) but doesn't project multiple
397	  future calls or their compounding cache effects.
398	- Feasibility is a hard cutoff (`0.0`) rather than a graduated penalty near the context limit, and
399	  per the point above it is evaluated against the cumulative total, not the real next-prompt size.
400	
401	### Performance
402	
403	- No quality labels exist in the export. Any performance score is a **proxy** — derive it from
404	  observable structure (platform inferred from the toolset, trajectory length, tool-call density,
405	  error and retry patterns in tool outputs), or from judge-model rescoring of individual calls.
406	  `Trajectory.normalized_items` is there so a proxy can be derived without re-parsing the export.
407	- **Check every candidate proxy against the leakage table in §4 first.** Coding dialect, item
408	  encoding, `custom_tool_call`, `reasoning`, and an empty final message are all `served_model`
409	  wearing a hat.
410	- **`submit_draft` is not a completion signal.** It is the human-approval gate: Viktor prepares a
411	  consequential action as a draft, a human approves it in thread state, and `submit_draft`
412	  executes it (the output names the real tool behind the gate, e.g. `mcp_google_ads_remove_ad`).
413	  It is offered in all 1,000 requests but invoked in only **14**, 37 calls total, and never as a
414	  terminator. Read it as "performed a gated, irreversible action" — a task-type signal at ~1.4%
415	  prevalence, not a success signal.
416	- Judge-model rescoring is permitted with the team's own API keys, but the core pipeline must
417	  stay runnable **offline on a laptop, with no GPU and no API keys required**.
418	
419	### Aggregation
420	
421	`model.py` owns the weighted average, the ranking, and the HOLD/CHANGE decision. Keep the
422	weights a parameter threaded through the call, not a module-level constant — sweeping them is
423	how the cost–quality frontier gets produced, and the frontier is the headline artifact.
424	
425	---
426	
427	## 6. Evaluating the router (the hard part)
428	
429	The log shows only the model that actually ran. Estimating what a *different* route would have
430	cost or delivered is off-policy evaluation, and it is the depth of this challenge — matching or
431	weighting across comparable trajectories, judge-model rescoring of single calls.
432	
433	Naming where your estimate can fail is **scored, not penalized**. The deliverable is a
434	cost–quality frontier, not a single point, and a five-minute presentation with one chart, one
435	claim, and one known weakness.

442	  section in the same commit. The next agent has no other design doc to read.

444	- **Enrich, don't replace.** Scoring stages set attributes on the `ModelLLM` objects they are

content.text:
I read `router_models/price_model.py`, the README §5 spec it implements, `data_models/Trajectory.py`/`ModelLLM`, `pre_processing/trajectory_analyzer.py` (where the fields are actually computed), and ran the test suite (10/10 pass). Overall: **solid**. The core idea — model the "cache trap" (a switch resets the provider's prefix cache and re-pays the whole accumulated prefix) as the dominant cost driver, then min-max normalize within the candidate pool — is the right framing for this problem, and the commit you just made genuinely fixes a real bug (the old code derived `total_tokens - total_cached_tokens` and then double-counted the same tokens as "not yet cached" and "fully cached"). The new version keeps `total_tokens` and `total_cached_tokens` as two distinct fields instead of re-deriving one from the other, which is correct per their own field docstrings.

Strengths:
- HOLD vs. CHANGE split is correct: HOLD bills `total_cached_tokens` at the cached rate and the remainder + increment at full rate; CHANGE bills the entire next input at full rate. That reproduces the trap directly — I verified `test_cache_makes_holding_cheaper_than_an_equally_priced_switch` and `test_much_cheaper_switch_can_still_beat_holding` both hold algebraically.
- Feasibility gate is handled cleanly — infeasible candidates get `0.0` and are excluded from the min-max range so they don't compress everyone else's spread.
- Simplifications (cumulative `total_tokens` standing in for "next call size", same-trajectory average for the increment) are stated explicitly in the README rather than hidden, which is exactly right for a challenge deliverable.
- Tests are well-targeted: partial/full/no cache, hold-vs-switch tie when there's no cache to lose, and the infeasibility path — arithmetic pinned with exact expected values, not just "score went up."

One real nit worth fixing, one worth just noting:

1. **`increment_tokens` duplicates `avg_input_tokens_per_call`.** `price_model.py` computes `accumulated_context_tokens / trajectory.total_calls` itself, but `trajectory_analyzer.py:291` already sets `avg_input_tokens_per_call = per_call(total_tokens)` — the identical formula. Right now they can't drift (same formula, same inputs), but `price_model.py` is silently re-deriving a value that already exists as a named field instead of reading `trajectory.avg_input_tokens_per_call` directly. If the analyzer's definition of that field ever changes, price_model would quietly diverge. Cheap fix, worth doing.

2. **The "increment" name overstates what's being estimated**, and the bias has a knowable direction the README doesn't quantify. `total_tokens / total_calls` is the *average* per-call prompt size across the whole trajectory, not the marginal growth between consecutive calls. For a roughly linearly-growing prefix (each call adds ~constant new content `g`), the average of the cumulative sums is ~`g·(n+1)/2` — i.e., this can overestimate the true next-call increment by roughly 2x on longer trajectories, not just "mis-estimated" as the README currently says. Since this term is added identically to both HOLD's and CHANGE's uncached tally, it mostly cancels out when comparing HOLD vs. a same-priced CHANGE, but it does *not* cancel when candidates have different `input_price_per_1m`, so it can still nudge the ranking among CHANGE candidates. Not a blocker, but worth a one-line addition to "Known simplifications" quantifying the direction/magnitude rather than leaving it vague.

Neither is a correctness bug in the sense the last commit fixed — no double-counting, no leaked `served_model` signal, normalization is sound. I'd ship this as-is and treat #1 as a quick cleanup; #2 is worth a doc sentence but not worth complicating the formula for a v1.

You could — today, `total_cached_tokens` is always `≤ total_tokens` by construction. In `trajectory_analyzer.py:260-262`:

```python
total_cached_tokens = int((total_tokens - prompt_tokens[-1]) * CACHE_HIT_RATE) if prompt_tokens else 0
```

Since `CACHE_HIT_RATE` defaults to `1.0` and `prompt_tokens[-1] >= 0`, that's always `<= total_tokens`. So for data that actually comes out of the analyzer, the `min()` never changes anything.

But nothing enforces that invariant at the type level. `Trajectory` in `data_models/Trajectory.py` has no cross-field validator — `total_cached_tokens` is just `ge=0`, same as `total_tokens`. Two things make relying on "the analyzer guarantees it" fragile:

1. **`CACHE_HIT_RATE` is explicitly called out in the README as the one knob meant to be swept** ("that constant is the single place the assumption lives — sweep it from `price_model.py`"). If it's ever set `> 1.0` for an experiment, `total_cached_tokens` can exceed `total_tokens` for short trajectories where `prompt_tokens[-1]` is small.
2. `price_model.py`'s own module docstring says it's "a pure function of `(Trajectory, List[ModelLLM])`" — and your test file proves the point: `make_trajectory()` sets `total_tokens` and `total_cached_tokens` as independent, uncoupled kwargs with no derivation step. Any future caller (synthetic data, a different ingestion path, a hand-built `Trajectory`) can violate the invariant just as easily.

If you drop the `min()` and someone does pass `total_cached_tokens > accumulated_context_tokens`, `uncached_tokens = (accumulated_context_tokens - cached_tokens) + increment_tokens` goes negative, and that negative token count gets multiplied by `input_price_per_1m` — producing a negative cost that would silently corrupt the min-max normalization (a broken-data candidate could look like the cheapest option instead of failing loudly).

So: the `min()` isn't defending against real analyzer output, it's defending the module's stated contract (pure function of whatever `Trajectory` it's handed) against an invariant that lives in a different file's arithmetic, not in the schema. I'd keep it — one line of insurance is cheap next to a silent negative-cost bug.
okay. but the calculations are correct?

Yes. I hand-traced the arithmetic against the spec and the tests, and it holds up:

- **Formula matches README §5 exactly**: shape the next call from `total_tokens`/`total_cached_tokens`/`total_calls`/`avg_output_tokens_per_call` alone → feasibility gate → HOLD splits cached/uncached, CHANGE bills everything uncached → cost in USD → min-max normalize over feasible candidates. No step is skipped or reordered.
- **I re-derived the numbers by hand**, not just trusted the test's own assertion. E.g. test 1 (`total_tokens=10_000, total_cached_tokens=7_000, total_calls=5`): increment = 10,000/5 = 2,000; HOLD's cached = min(7,000, 10,000) = 7,000; uncached = (10,000−7,000)+2,000 = 5,000. Cost = (5,000×2.0 + 7,000×0.2)/1e6 = (10,000+1,400)/1e6 = $0.0114 — matches what the code produces.
- **`python -m unittest discover -s tests` → 10/10 pass**, covering partial cache, full cache, zero cache (hold == switch, no cache to lose), switch-bills-everything-uncached, cache-makes-holding-cheaper, a cheap-enough-switch-still-wins case, infeasibility → `None`, and the normalization edge cases (tie → both 1.0, infeasible excluded from the min-max range).
- No leakage: it only reads `trajectory.served_model` for the hold/switch check, which the README's shared contract explicitly permits — it's not reading anything that proxies task quality or the log's actual outcome.

So: correct relative to its own spec, correct arithmetic, correct test coverage. The caveats from before (the `min()` cap, the `increment_tokens` naming/magnitude issue) are about *what the formula chooses to approximate*, not about it computing its own approximation wrong — those are documented simplifications, not calculation errors.
does it make senseß

Mostly yes — the core idea is sound: for a router picking a model for the *next* call, the switch-resets-the-cache dynamic really is the dominant cost effect on long trajectories, and modeling HOLD vs. CHANGE asymmetrically around that is the right call. The relative comparison (holding beats an equally-priced switch, a cheap-enough switch can still win) behaves the way you'd want a price signal to behave.

The one place I'd push back on conceptually, not just as an implementation nit: using `total_tokens` (the *cumulative sum* of every past call's prompt size) as the stand-in for "the next call's input size" isn't a small rounding error — for a trajectory that's grown roughly linearly over `n` calls, that sum overstates the actual next prompt by roughly a factor of `n/2` (the README's own example: a 20-call, 1M-token trajectory's real next prompt is ~50K, not 1M+). That inflation feeds two places:

1. **The dollar estimate** — fuzzy but survivable, since it inflates every candidate's cost roughly proportionally.
2. **The feasibility gate** — not survivable in the same way. A model with a genuinely adequate context window for the real next call can get hard-zeroed (`price_score = 0.0`) because the *cumulative* total trips its window limit, even though it would serve the actual next request fine. That doesn't just blur the price estimate, it can remove a legitimately cheap, viable candidate from consideration entirely — which is a bigger deal for a router than dollar noise.

That tradeoff is already named in the README's "Known simplifications," so it's not hidden, and I get the appeal (keeps the formula a pure function of `Trajectory` fields with no extra assumptions). But if context-window differences between your candidate models are meaningfully different sizes, I'd treat this as the thing most worth revisiting before the frontier chart goes in the deck — everything else about the approach holds up.
but every time you send a message you have to resend everything, so isnt that right?

The "resend everything" mechanic is real, but it applies to *each individual call*, not to the running sum. That distinction is exactly where `total_tokens` stops being a good stand-in for "the next call's size."

Concretely, from `trajectory_analyzer.py:253`: `prompt_tokens[i]` for call *i* already **is** the full resent history up through that point — that's your intuition, and it's correct. But `total_tokens` isn't any single `prompt_tokens[i]`; it's `sum(prompt_tokens)` — the sum of *every* call's already-resent snapshot, across all `n` calls.

Small example to make it concrete. Say each call adds ~10 tokens of genuinely new content, and every call resends everything before it:

- call 1 prompt: 10
- call 2 prompt: resends call 1 (10) + call 1's response + 10 new ≈ 30
- call 3 prompt: resends call 2's whole thing (30) + response + 10 new ≈ 50

`total_tokens = 10 + 30 + 50 = 90`. But the *actual next call* (call 4) only has to resend call 3's full history (≈50) plus its response plus new content — something like 60-70, not 90. The 90 double-, triple-counts content that got superseded by later, bigger snapshots: call 1's 10 tokens are baked into call 2's 30, which are baked into call 3's 50, and `total_tokens` adds all three snapshots up instead of just reporting the latest (largest) one.

"""Assign `price_score` to each candidate `ModelLLM` for one `Trajectory`.

Per the README's scoring contract (§5): `price_score` is `[0, 1]`, higher = cheaper,
normalized *within this trajectory's candidate pool* — not against some global price
scale. This module is a pure function of `(Trajectory, List[ModelLLM])`; the only place
it reads `Trajectory.served_model` is the switching-cost check below, which the README
explicitly carves out as legitimate (it is not a task-quality proxy).

The crux, per README §5: providers cache the shared input prefix across a trajectory's
calls, and a model switch resets that cache. So "cheaper per token" and "cheaper for
the next call" are different questions once a trajectory has accumulated context — a
model switch pays full uncached price for the whole next prompt, which in long
trajectories can dwarf any per-token saving. That's the entire reason this module needs
`served_model` at all: to tell a HOLD's mostly-cached next call apart from a CHANGE's
fully-uncached one.

The base for "how big is the next prompt" is `Trajectory.last_call_input_tokens`, not
`total_tokens` -- see `_next_call_tokens` for why: every call resends the whole history
up to that point, so the next call's size tracks the size of the *most recent* call, not
the sum of every past call's own (already-superseded) full-history snapshot.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from data_models.model_llm import ModelLLM
from data_models.Trajectory import Trajectory


def _next_call_tokens(trajectory: Trajectory) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
    """ESTIMATE the shape of the trajectory's next call.

    Returns (last_call_input_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens).

    `last_call_input_tokens` is `Trajectory.last_call_input_tokens` taken at face value:
    the size of the most recently recovered call's full prompt (tool schemas + history
    up to that point). Because every call resends the whole history, this is the best
    available proxy for the size of the *next* call's prompt.

    This deliberately does NOT use `total_tokens`. `total_tokens` sums every past call's
    prompt -- each of which was itself a full-history resend at the time -- so it adds up
    several superseded snapshots of a growing thing instead of reporting the size of the
    latest one. On a trajectory whose prompt grows roughly linearly over `n` calls,
    `total_tokens` overstates the real next-call size by very roughly a factor of `n/2`,
    and can trip the context-window feasibility gate below for a model that would
    actually serve the real next call fine. `last_call_input_tokens` doesn't have that
    problem: it's one call's real size, not an accumulating sum.

    `increment_tokens` approximates how much *new* content (tool outputs, replies, ...)
    a typical call in this trajectory appends, as the trajectory's own average per-call
    growth (`total_tokens / total_calls`). There is no better signal available: the next
    call's actual new content is by definition not in the log yet. This average is a
    separate, smaller known simplification (it can over- or under-estimate a single
    step depending on whether the trajectory's growth is front- or back-loaded) --
    see the README's "Known simplifications".
    """
    last_call_input_tokens = float(trajectory.last_call_input_tokens)
    increment_tokens = (
        float(trajectory.total_tokens) / trajectory.total_calls if trajectory.total_calls else 0.0
    )
    next_output_tokens = trajectory.avg_output_tokens_per_call
    return last_call_input_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens


def _next_call_cost(trajectory: Trajectory, model: ModelLLM) -> float | None:
    """ESTIMATE the USD cost of `model` serving this trajectory's next call.

    Returns None if `model.context_window_size` can't hold the next call at all --
    that candidate is infeasible, not merely expensive, and is handled separately. This
    gate is now evaluated against `last_call_input_tokens` (the real next-prompt
    estimate), not the whole trajectory's cumulative footprint, so a long trajectory no
    longer trips it for a model that would comfortably serve the actual next call.
    """
    last_call_input_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens = _next_call_tokens(
        trajectory
    )
    next_input_tokens = last_call_input_tokens + increment_tokens

    if next_input_tokens + next_output_tokens > model.context_window_size:
        return None

    holding = model.name == trajectory.served_model
    if holding:
        # Same model as the log: the last call's whole prompt was already sent once and
        # is cache-eligible; only the new increment is guaranteed uncached. Cap at
        # `last_call_input_tokens` -- `total_cached_tokens` is a whole-trajectory
        # aggregate and can exceed the size of any single call, but only that much of it
        # is actually part of *this* call's bill.
        cached_tokens = min(float(trajectory.total_cached_tokens), last_call_input_tokens)
        uncached_tokens = (last_call_input_tokens - cached_tokens) + increment_tokens
    else:
        # A switch resets the provider's prefix cache: the whole next prompt is
        # uncached, not just the increment. This is the cache trap from README §5.
        cached_tokens = 0.0
        uncached_tokens = next_input_tokens

    input_cost = (
        uncached_tokens * model.input_price_per_1m
        + cached_tokens * model.cached_input_price_per_1m
    ) / 1_000_000
    output_cost = next_output_tokens * model.output_price_per_1m / 1_000_000
    return input_cost + output_cost


def score_price(trajectory: Trajectory, models: list[ModelLLM]) -> list[ModelLLM]:
    """Enrich each `ModelLLM` in `models` with a `price_score` in `[0, 1]`.

    Higher is cheaper. Costs are estimated per `_next_call_cost` and min-max
    normalized across `models` — this trajectory's candidate pool only, per README
    §5's "normalize within the candidate pool, not globally". Infeasible candidates
    (next call wouldn't fit their context window) are scored 0.0 and excluded from the
    min-max range so one unusable model doesn't compress everyone else's spread.
    """
    costs: dict[str, float | None] = {
        model.name: _next_call_cost(trajectory, model) for model in models
    }

    feasible_costs = [cost for cost in costs.values() if cost is not None]
    if not feasible_costs:
        for model in models:
            model.price_score = 0.0
        return models

    cheapest, priciest = min(feasible_costs), max(feasible_costs)
    spread = priciest - cheapest

    for model in models:
        cost = costs[model.name]
        if cost is None:
            model.price_score = 0.0
        elif spread == 0:
            model.price_score = 1.0
        else:
            model.price_score = (priciest - cost) / spread

    return models

from data_models.Trajectory import Trajectory, ViktorEnvironment

def make_model(name: str, **overrides) -> ModelLLM:

        name=name,
        family=name,
        context_window_size=1_000_000,
        input_price_per_1m=2.0,
        cached_input_price_per_1m=0.2,
        output_price_per_1m=10.0,
        cached_output_price_per_1m=0.0,

    return ModelLLM(**defaults)


def make_trajectory(**overrides) -> Trajectory:

            served_model="model-a",

            total_calls=5,
            last_call_input_tokens=3_000,

        model = make_model("model-a", output_price_per_1m=0.0)  # isolate input-side math

        cost = _next_call_cost(trajectory, model)

        expected = (3_200 * 2.0 + 1_800 * 0.2) / 1_000_000

        # call's bill, so it must be capped, not applied wholesale.

            served_model="model-a",

            total_cached_tokens=100_000,
            total_calls=10,

1	"""Assign `price_score` to each candidate `ModelLLM` for one `Trajectory`.
2	
3	Per the README's scoring contract (§5): `price_score` is `[0, 1]`, higher = cheaper,
4	normalized *within this trajectory's candidate pool* — not against some global price
5	scale. This module is a pure function of `(Trajectory, List[ModelLLM])`; the only place
6	it reads `Trajectory.served_model` is the switching-cost check below, which the README
7	explicitly carves out as legitimate (it is not a task-quality proxy).
8	
9	The crux, per README §5: providers cache the shared input prefix across a trajectory's
10	calls, and a model switch resets that cache. So "cheaper per token" and "cheaper for
11	the next call" are different questions once a trajectory has accumulated context — a
12	model switch pays full uncached price for the whole next prompt, which in long
13	trajectories can dwarf any per-token saving. That's the entire reason this module needs
14	`served_model` at all: to tell a HOLD's mostly-cached next call apart from a CHANGE's
15	fully-uncached one.
16	
17	The base for "how big is the next prompt" is `Trajectory.last_call_input_tokens`, not
18	`total_tokens` -- see `_next_call_tokens` for why: every call resends the whole history
19	up to that point, so the next call's size tracks the size of the *most recent* call, not
20	the sum of every past call's own (already-superseded) full-history snapshot.
21	"""
22	
23	from __future__ import annotations
24	
25	from data_models.model_llm import ModelLLM
26	from data_models.Trajectory import Trajectory
27	
28	
29	def _next_call_tokens(trajectory: Trajectory) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
30	    """ESTIMATE the shape of the trajectory's next call.
31	
32	    Returns (last_call_input_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens).
33	
34	    `last_call_input_tokens` is `Trajectory.last_call_input_tokens` taken at face value:
35	    the size of the most recently recovered call's full prompt (tool schemas + history
36	    up to that point). Because every call resends the whole history, this is the best
37	    available proxy for the size of the *next* call's prompt.
38	
39	    This deliberately does NOT use `total_tokens`. `total_tokens` sums every past call's
40	    prompt -- each of which was itself a full-history resend at the time -- so it adds up
41	    several superseded snapshots of a growing thing instead of reporting the size of the
42	    latest one. On a trajectory whose prompt grows roughly linearly over `n` calls,
43	    `total_tokens` overstates the real next-call size by very roughly a factor of `n/2`,
44	    and can trip the context-window feasibility gate below for a model that would
45	    actually serve the real next call fine. `last_call_input_tokens` doesn't have that
46	    problem: it's one call's real size, not an accumulating sum.
47	
48	    `increment_tokens` approximates how much *new* content (tool outputs, replies, ...)
49	    a typical call in this trajectory appends, as the trajectory's own average per-call
50	    growth (`last_call_input_tokens / total_calls`) -- not `total_tokens / total_calls`,
51	    which is the same superseded-snapshots mistake `last_call_input_tokens` exists to
52	    avoid, just applied to the increment instead of the prompt size: it averages in
53	    every past call's own (smaller, since-outgrown) prompt size, not how much this
54	    trajectory actually grows per step. There is no better signal available for the
55	    increment itself: the next call's actual new content is by definition not in the
56	    log yet. This average is a separate, smaller known simplification (it can over- or
57	    under-estimate a single step depending on whether the trajectory's growth is
58	    front- or back-loaded) -- see the README's "Known simplifications".
59	    """
60	    last_call_input_tokens = float(trajectory.last_call_input_tokens)
61	    increment_tokens = (
62	        last_call_input_tokens / trajectory.total_calls if trajectory.total_calls else 0.0
63	    )
64	    next_output_tokens = trajectory.avg_output_tokens_per_call
65	    return last_call_input_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens
66	
67	
68	def _next_call_cost(trajectory: Trajectory, model: ModelLLM) -> float | None:
69	    """ESTIMATE the USD cost of `model` serving this trajectory's next call.
70	
71	    Returns None if `model.context_window_size` can't hold the next call at all --
72	    that candidate is infeasible, not merely expensive, and is handled separately. This
73	    gate is now evaluated against `last_call_input_tokens` (the real next-prompt
74	    estimate), not the whole trajectory's cumulative footprint, so a long trajectory no
75	    longer trips it for a model that would comfortably serve the actual next call.
76	    """
77	    last_call_input_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens = _next_call_tokens(
78	        trajectory
79	    )
80	    next_input_tokens = last_call_input_tokens + increment_tokens
81	
82	    if next_input_tokens + next_output_tokens > model.context_window_size:
83	        return None
84	
85	    holding = model.name == trajectory.served_model
86	    if holding:
87	        # Same model as the log: the last call's whole prompt was already sent once and
88	        # is cache-eligible; only the new increment is guaranteed uncached. Cap at
89	        # `last_call_input_tokens` -- `total_cached_tokens` is a whole-trajectory
90	        # aggregate and can exceed the size of any single call, but only that much of it
91	        # is actually part of *this* call's bill.
92	        cached_tokens = min(float(trajectory.total_cached_tokens), last_call_input_tokens)
93	        uncached_tokens = (last_call_input_tokens - cached_tokens) + increment_tokens
94	    else:
95	        # A switch resets the provider's prefix cache: the whole next prompt is
96	        # uncached, not just the increment. This is the cache trap from README §5.
97	        cached_tokens = 0.0
98	        uncached_tokens = next_input_tokens
99	
100	    input_cost = (
101	        uncached_tokens * model.input_price_per_1m
102	        + cached_tokens * model.cached_input_price_per_1m
103	    ) / 1_000_000
104	    output_cost = next_output_tokens * model.output_price_per_1m / 1_000_000
105	    return input_cost + output_cost
106	
107	
108	def score_price(trajectory: Trajectory, models: list[ModelLLM]) -> list[ModelLLM]:
109	    """Enrich each `ModelLLM` in `models` with a `price_score` in `[0, 1]`.
110	
111	    Higher is cheaper. Costs are estimated per `_next_call_cost` and min-max
112	    normalized across `models` — this trajectory's candidate pool only, per README
113	    §5's "normalize within the candidate pool, not globally". Infeasible candidates
114	    (next call wouldn't fit their context window) are scored 0.0 and excluded from the
115	    min-max range so one unusable model doesn't compress everyone else's spread.
116	    """
117	    costs: dict[str, float | None] = {
118	        model.name: _next_call_cost(trajectory, model) for model in models
119	    }
120	
121	    feasible_costs = [cost for cost in costs.values() if cost is not None]
122	    if not feasible_costs:
123	        for model in models:
124	            model.price_score = 0.0
125	        return models
126	
127	    cheapest, priciest = min(feasible_costs), max(feasible_costs)
128	    spread = priciest - cheapest
129	
130	    for model in models:
131	        cost = costs[model.name]
132	        if cost is None:
133	            model.price_score = 0.0
134	        elif spread == 0:
135	            model.price_score = 1.0
136	        else:
137	            model.price_score = (priciest - cost) / spread
138	
139	    return models
140

"""Assign `price_score` to each candidate `ModelLLM` for one `Trajectory`.

Per the README's scoring contract (§5): `price_score` is `[0, 1]`, higher = cheaper,
normalized *within this trajectory's candidate pool* — not against some global price
scale. This module is a pure function of `(Trajectory, List[ModelLLM])`; the only place
it reads `Trajectory.served_model` is the switching-cost check below, which the README
explicitly carves out as legitimate (it is not a task-quality proxy).

The crux, per README §5: providers cache the shared input prefix across a trajectory's
calls, and a model switch resets that cache. So "cheaper per token" and "cheaper for
the next call" are different questions once a trajectory has accumulated context — a
model switch pays full uncached price for the whole next prompt, which in long
trajectories can dwarf any per-token saving. That's the entire reason this module needs
`served_model` at all: to tell a HOLD's mostly-cached next call apart from a CHANGE's
fully-uncached one.

The base for "how big is the next prompt" is `Trajectory.last_call_input_tokens`, not
`total_tokens` -- see `_next_call_tokens` for why: every call resends the whole history
up to that point, so the next call's size tracks the size of the *most recent* call, not
the sum of every past call's own (already-superseded) full-history snapshot.

No candidate is ever excluded for having too small a context window. If the next call
wouldn't fit, `_next_call_cost` assumes the context gets compacted down to whatever the
model can hold -- see its docstring for how that interacts with caching.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from data_models.model_llm import ModelLLM
from data_models.Trajectory import Trajectory


def _next_call_tokens(trajectory: Trajectory) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
    """ESTIMATE the shape of the trajectory's next call.

    Returns (last_call_input_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens).

    `last_call_input_tokens` is `Trajectory.last_call_input_tokens` taken at face value:
    the size of the most recently recovered call's full prompt (tool schemas + history
    up to that point). Because every call resends the whole history, this is the best
    available proxy for the size of the *next* call's prompt.

    This deliberately does NOT use `total_tokens`. `total_tokens` sums every past call's
    prompt -- each of which was itself a full-history resend at the time -- so it adds up
    several superseded snapshots of a growing thing instead of reporting the size of the
    latest one. On a trajectory whose prompt grows roughly linearly over `n` calls,
    `total_tokens` overstates the real next-call size by very roughly a factor of `n/2`.
    `last_call_input_tokens` doesn't have that problem: it's one call's real size, not an
    accumulating sum.

    `increment_tokens` approximates how much *new* content (tool outputs, replies, ...)
    a typical call in this trajectory appends, as the trajectory's own average per-call
    growth (`last_call_input_tokens / total_calls`) -- not `total_tokens / total_calls`,
    which is the same superseded-snapshots mistake `last_call_input_tokens` exists to
    avoid, just applied to the increment instead of the prompt size: it averages in
    every past call's own (smaller, since-outgrown) prompt size, not how much this
    trajectory actually grows per step. There is no better signal available for the
    increment itself: the next call's actual new content is by definition not in the
    log yet. This average is a separate, smaller known simplification (it can over- or
    under-estimate a single step depending on whether the trajectory's growth is
    front- or back-loaded) -- see the README's "Known simplifications".
    """
    last_call_input_tokens = float(trajectory.last_call_input_tokens)
    increment_tokens = (
        last_call_input_tokens / trajectory.total_calls if trajectory.total_calls else 0.0
    )
    next_output_tokens = trajectory.avg_output_tokens_per_call
    return last_call_input_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens


def _next_call_cost(trajectory: Trajectory, model: ModelLLM) -> float:
    """ESTIMATE the USD cost of `model` serving this trajectory's next call.

    Never excludes a candidate for having too small a context window. If the estimated
    next call (input + output) doesn't fit, this assumes the context gets compacted
    (summarized) down to whatever room is available -- output first, since a model can
    never emit more than its own window regardless of compaction, then input with
    whatever room remains. A compacted input is a rewritten prompt, not the original
    text, so the provider's cached prefix no longer matches it: nothing is cached on a
    compacted call, holding or switching alike -- `total_cached_tokens` describes a cache
    for the *uncompacted* history, which this call by definition isn't sending.
    """
    last_call_input_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens = _next_call_tokens(
        trajectory
    )
    next_input_tokens = last_call_input_tokens + increment_tokens

    billed_output_tokens = min(next_output_tokens, model.context_window_size)
    room_for_input = model.context_window_size - billed_output_tokens

    if next_input_tokens > room_for_input:
        # Compacted: the whole prompt was rewritten to fit, so none of it matches
        # whatever the provider had cached from the real history.
        cached_tokens = 0.0
        uncached_tokens = room_for_input
    else:
        holding = model.name == trajectory.served_model
        if holding:
            # Same model as the log: the last call's whole prompt was already sent once
            # and is cache-eligible; only the new increment is guaranteed uncached. Cap
            # at `last_call_input_tokens` -- `total_cached_tokens` is a whole-trajectory
            # aggregate and can exceed the size of any single call, but only that much
            # of it is actually part of *this* call's bill.
            cached_tokens = min(float(trajectory.total_cached_tokens), last_call_input_tokens)
            uncached_tokens = (last_call_input_tokens - cached_tokens) + increment_tokens
        else:
            # A switch resets the provider's prefix cache: the whole next prompt is
            # uncached, not just the increment. This is the cache trap from README §5.
            cached_tokens = 0.0
            uncached_tokens = next_input_tokens

    input_cost = (
        uncached_tokens * model.input_price_per_1m
        + cached_tokens * model.cached_input_price_per_1m
    ) / 1_000_000
    output_cost = billed_output_tokens * model.output_price_per_1m / 1_000_000
    return input_cost + output_cost


def score_price(trajectory: Trajectory, models: list[ModelLLM]) -> list[ModelLLM]:
    """Enrich each `ModelLLM` in `models` with a `price_score` in `[0, 1]`.

    Higher is cheaper. Costs are estimated per `_next_call_cost` and min-max normalized
    across `models` — this trajectory's candidate pool only, per README §5's "normalize
    within the candidate pool, not globally". Every candidate gets a real cost (small
    context windows are compacted to fit, never excluded — see `_next_call_cost`), so
    the min-max range always covers every model in the pool.
    """
    costs = {model.name: _next_call_cost(trajectory, model) for model in models}

    cheapest, priciest = min(costs.values()), max(costs.values())
    spread = priciest - cheapest

    for model in models:
        cost = costs[model.name]
        if spread == 0:
            model.price_score = 1.0
        else:
            model.price_score = (priciest - cost) / spread

    return models

lets do the following. for the quality we need a base value, because if all models have different answers, we need a value we can rely on. so create a new file in the data_model folder called quality_base_value.py. it should contain 4 dictionaries, one with qualitiy value of the models from the following benchmark: https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/artificial-analysis-intelligence-index; then from https://arena.ai/leaderboard/agent and from https://arena.ai/leaderboard/text. then the fourth dictionary contain a value from 0-1 with 1 being the model with the best scores in the benchmarks. keep in mind that all benchmarks should have the same weight. Also update our readme in the  part of the quality score saying that we have a base score in case all models have different answers. Also read this to contextualize yourself: We assign each LLM a quality score in [0, 1] used for model selection/weighting. The score is derived from existing public benchmarks (not our own vibes) so it's reproducible and defensible. It reflects peak capability (highest effort setting available per model).

Sources. We aggregate three independent leaderboards, each measuring a different axis of "quality":

Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (v4.1.1) — https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/artificial-analysis-intelligence-index
Automated capability benchmark. AA runs 9 fixed evaluations itself (GDPval-AA, Terminal-Bench, SciCode, Humanity's Last Exam, GPQA Diamond, CritPt, τ³-Banking, AA-Omniscience, AA-LCR) under standardized conditions, scores pass@1, and takes a weighted average scaled 0–100. Weighting is agentic-heavy: 34% agents, 24% coding, 24% scientific reasoning, 18% general. Answers the question: does it solve hard, verifiable tasks?
Agent Arena — https://arena.ai/leaderboard/agent
Real-world agentic performance. No voting. Every live "Agent Mode" session (with terminal/web/filesystem tools) is routed to a randomly chosen model, creating a randomized controlled trial. Causal inference ("causal tracing") then estimates each model's treatment effect vs. the average model across 5 signals (confirmed success, praise vs. complaint, steerability, bash recovery, tool hallucination). The headline metric is Net Improvement (percentage points vs. average). Answers: does using this model make real work turn out better?
Text Arena / LMArena — https://arena.ai/leaderboard/text
Human preference. Users get two anonymous responses to a live prompt and vote for the better one; scores come from a Bradley-Terry model with style control (removes the advantage of longer/prettier answers). Answers: do humans prefer its responses?

Why these three. They're not redundant — they measure partially independent things, and they disagree in informative ways (e.g., older Opus ranks below newer models on AA capability but above them on human preference). Three benefits:

Coverage: capability, real-world outcomes, and subjective preference are all part of "quality"; no single board captures all three.
Error cancellation: each board has its own bias (AA can be over-fit/STEM-heavy, Text rewards likeability, Agent reflects Arena's user mix). Because the biases differ, averaging dilutes the noise and reinforces the shared "real quality" signal.
Hard to game: a model can spoof one number, but the exploits differ across boards — leading all three requires being genuinely good at all three.

"""A quality **base value** per known model id, derived from public leaderboards.

Per README §5 ("Performance"), no quality labels exist in the export — any
`performance_score` is necessarily a proxy. This module is the fallback layer beneath
that proxy: when a trajectory's own signal is ambiguous or candidates disagree, the
router needs *something* to fall back on that isn't a vibe. These four dictionaries are
that something — a quality prior derived from three independent, public, reproducible
benchmarks rather than this project's own judgment.

Snapshot captured 2026-08-23 from the live leaderboards below. All three are dashboards
that move as providers ship new checkpoints, so these numbers are a point-in-time
reading, not a fixed fact — re-scrape and rebuild this file if the scores drift enough to
matter. Every score records the specific model *variant* (reasoning-effort setting) the
leaderboard listed it under, because none of these boards guarantee one row per model
family — see the per-entry comments below.

Sources (one dict each), all restricted to the 9 model ids this project's candidate pool
uses (`pre_processing/model_list.py`'s `_MODEL_FAMILIES`):

1. **Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (v4.1.1)**
   https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/artificial-analysis-intelligence-index
   Automated capability benchmark (9 fixed evals, pass@1, weighted 0-100). Answers: does
   it solve hard, verifiable tasks?
2. **Agent Arena** — https://arena.ai/leaderboard/agent
   Real-world agentic performance via causal tracing over live "Agent Mode" sessions.
   Headline metric: Net Improvement, percentage points vs. the average model. Answers:
   does using this model make real work turn out better?
3. **Text Arena / LMArena** — https://arena.ai/leaderboard/text
   Human preference: blind pairwise votes, Bradley-Terry model with style control.
   Answers: do humans prefer its responses?

Why these three and not one: they measure partially independent things (capability,
real-world outcome, subjective preference), each has its own bias (AA can run
STEM-heavy, Text rewards likeability, Agent reflects Arena's own user mix), and gaming
all three at once is much harder than gaming one. Equal-weighting them lets the biases
cancel instead of compounding — see `QUALITY_BASE_SCORE` below for how that weighting is
actually applied.

Every score below reflects **peak capability**: the highest reasoning-effort variant of
each model that the given leaderboard listed a score for, not necessarily the same
effort setting across benchmarks (a board that only ever tested one variant of a model
gets that variant; a board that tested several gets the best of those).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

# --- 1. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index ------------------------------------
#
# Scale: 0-100, higher is better. One score per model; AA's page for each model lists
# only the reasoning-effort variant(s) it evaluated, so "peak" here is whatever AA itself
# scored highest for that model id (never a different provider-side variant AA didn't
# test) -- see the inline comment on each row for the exact labeled variant used.
AA_INTELLIGENCE_INDEX: dict[str, float] = {
    "claude-opus-5": 63,        # "Claude Opus 5 (Adaptive Reasoning, Max Effort / Xhigh Effort)" -- both 63
    "claude-opus-4-8": 57,      # "Claude Opus 4.8 (Adaptive Reasoning, Max Effort)"
    "claude-opus-4-6": 39,      # "Claude Opus 4.6 (Non-reasoning, High Effort)" -- only variant AA lists
    "claude-sonnet-5": 55,      # "Claude Sonnet 5 (Adaptive Reasoning, Max Effort)"
    "claude-sonnet-4-6": 37,    # "Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Non-reasoning)" -- deprecated model, only variant AA lists
    "claude-fable-5": 62,       # "Claude Fable 5 (Adaptive Reasoning, Max Effort, Opus 4.8 Fallback)"
    "gpt-5.6-sol": 61,          # "GPT-5.6 Sol (max)"
    "gpt-5.6-terra": 57,        # "GPT-5.6 Terra (max)"
    "gpt-5.6-luna": 52,         # "GPT-5.6 Luna (max)"
}

# --- 2. Agent Arena -----------------------------------------------------------------
#
# Scale: Net Improvement, percentage points vs. the average model (can be negative in
# general; every model in our pool happens to score positive). Higher is better. Several
# effort variants are listed per model on this board; the value here is the best-scoring
# variant for that model id.
AGENT_ARENA_NET_IMPROVEMENT: dict[str, float] = {
    "claude-opus-5": 12.47,     # "Claude Opus 5 (High)" -- beats "(Max)" at 12.00
    "claude-opus-4-8": 9.55,    # "Claude Opus 4.8 (High)" -- beats unlabeled variant at 2.51
    "claude-opus-4-6": 6.60,    # "Claude Opus 4.6" -- only variant listed
    "claude-sonnet-5": 6.62,    # "Claude Sonnet 5 (High)" -- only variant listed
    "claude-sonnet-4-6": 2.88,  # "Claude Sonnet 4.6" -- only variant listed
    "claude-fable-5": 11.57,    # "Claude Fable 5 (High)" -- only variant listed
    "gpt-5.6-sol": 9.74,        # "GPT 5.6 Sol (xHigh)"
    "gpt-5.6-terra": 3.19,      # "GPT 5.6 Terra (xHigh)"
    "gpt-5.6-luna": 4.04,       # "GPT 5.6 Luna (xHigh)"
}

# --- 3. Text Arena / LMArena ---------------------------------------------------------
#
# Scale: Bradley-Terry rating with style control (Elo-like; this snapshot's 9 values
# span roughly 1450-1510). Higher is better. Rows are keyed by exact model+variant slug
# on the leaderboard; the value here is the best-scoring slug for that model id.
TEXT_ARENA_RATING: dict[str, float] = {
    "claude-opus-5": 1493,      # "claude-opus-5-high" -- beats "claude-opus-5-max" at 1487
    "claude-opus-4-8": 1482,    # "claude-opus-4-8-high" -- beats unlabeled slug at 1473
    "claude-opus-4-6": 1504,    # "claude-opus-4-6-high" -- beats unlabeled slug at 1497
    "claude-sonnet-5": 1461,    # "claude-sonnet-5-high" -- only slug listed
    "claude-sonnet-4-6": 1472,  # "claude-sonnet-4-6" -- only slug listed
    "claude-fable-5": 1508,     # "claude-fable-5" -- only slug listed
    "gpt-5.6-sol": 1482,        # "gpt-5.6-sol-xhigh" -- only slug listed
    "gpt-5.6-terra": 1465,      # "gpt-5.6-terra-xhigh" -- only slug listed
    "gpt-5.6-luna": 1451,       # "gpt-5.6-luna-xhigh" -- only slug listed
}

# --- 4. Composite quality base score --------------------------------------------------
#
# Scale: [0, 1], 1.0 = best in this candidate pool, 0.0 = worst. Built in two passes so
# the three source benchmarks -- on wildly different native scales (0-100, a percentage,
# a ~1450-1510 rating) -- contribute *equally* rather than whichever has the widest raw
# numeric spread dominating a naive average:
#
#   1. Min-max normalize each of the three dicts above to [0, 1] **within this same
#      9-model pool** (worst id in that benchmark -> 0.0, best -> 1.0).
#   2. Average the three normalized values per model, unweighted (1/3 each, per "all
#      benchmarks should have the same weight"), then min-max normalize *that* composite
#      one more time so the top model in the pool lands at exactly 1.0 and the bottom at
#      exactly 0.0.
#
# This is a base value, not a substitute for `performance_score`: it has no idea which
# model is best for *this* trajectory, only which one benchmarks best in general. Use it
# as the fallback prior when a trajectory's own signal doesn't clearly favor one
# candidate -- see README §5.
QUALITY_BASE_SCORE: dict[str, float] = {
    "claude-fable-5": 1.0000,
    "claude-opus-5": 0.9476,
    "gpt-5.6-sol": 0.7257,
    "claude-opus-4-8": 0.6562,
    "claude-opus-4-6": 0.4106,
    "claude-sonnet-5": 0.3559,
    "gpt-5.6-terra": 0.2716,
    "gpt-5.6-luna": 0.1318,
    "claude-sonnet-4-6": 0.0000,
}

- No quality labels exist in the export. Any performance score is a **proxy** — derive it from

  error and retry patterns in tool outputs), or from judge-model rescoring of individual calls.

- **`data_models/quality_base_value.py` supplies a base quality value for when candidates disagree.**

  call — e.g. everything ties, or the trajectory is too short to have a real tool-error or
  retry-pattern signal yet. For those cases the router needs a fallback quality prior that isn't
  just "pick one" — `QUALITY_BASE_SCORE` in that module is exactly that: a `[0, 1]` value per model

how did you calculate the final values? what was the formula? because the values from the bechmarkings didnt go from 0 to 1

Here's the exact formula, step by step, using `claude-fable-5` as the worked example.

**Step 1 — min-max normalize each benchmark to `[0,1]`, separately, within the 9-model pool.**

The three raw benchmarks are on incompatible scales (AA is 0–100, Agent Arena is a percentage, Text Arena is a ~1450–1510 rating), so each one gets its own min-max normalization first:

```
normalized(model) = (raw(model) − min(raw across all 9)) / (max(raw across all 9) − min(raw across all 9))
```

For `claude-fable-5`:

| Benchmark | raw | min | max | normalized |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AA Intelligence Index | 62 | 37 (sonnet-4-6) | 63 (opus-5) | (62−37)/(63−37) = **0.9615** |
| Agent Arena | 11.57 | 2.88 (sonnet-4-6) | 12.47 (opus-5) | (11.57−2.88)/(12.47−2.88) = **0.9062** |
| Text Arena | 1508 | 1451 (gpt-luna) | 1508 (fable-5 itself) | (1508−1451)/(1508−1451) = **1.0000** |

This is why fable-5 hits exactly 1.0 on Text Arena — it's the highest Text Arena rating in the pool — but not on the other two, because `claude-opus-5` beats it on both AA (63 vs 62) and Agent Arena (12.47 vs 11.57).

**Step 2 — average the three normalized values, equal weight (1/3 each), no further rescaling.**

```
QUALITY_BASE_SCORE(model) = (norm_AA + norm_Agent + norm_Text) / 3
```

For `claude-fable-5`: (0.9615 + 0.9062 + 1.0000) / 3 = **0.9559**.

That's the final value — I don't renormalize the composite a second time. Your earlier correction was specifically to drop that second pass (which had been artificially stretching whoever led the composite up to exactly 1.0). Because no single model tops all three benchmarks simultaneously, no model in this pool actually reaches 1.0 — `claude-opus-5` (0.9123) leads AA and Agent Arena but loses Text Arena to fable-5, and vice versa, so both land under 1.0. `1.0` is a theoretical ceiling, not a value anyone here achieves.

26	Outputs: results/benchmark_trajectories.csv, results/total_cost.png
27	"""
28	
29	from __future__ import annotations
30	
31	import argparse
32	import csv
33	import sys
34	from pathlib import Path
35	
36	sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent))
37	
38	from data_models.model_llm import ModelLLM
39	from pre_processing.model_list import build_model_list
40	from pre_processing.trajectory_analyzer import analyze_file
41	from router_models import model as model_stage
42	from router_models.performance_model import score_performance
43	from router_models.price_model import estimate_costs, score_price
44	
45	STRONGEST_NAME = "claude-fable-5"  # highest BASE_CAPABILITY prior in the pool (priors.py)
46	CHEAPEST_NAME = "gpt-5.6-luna"     # lowest listed input rate in the pool
47	DEFAULT_WEIGHT = 0.1  # w_price for the router's single fixed operating point (w_perf =
48	# 1 - this). performance_score's dynamic range in this data is narrow (~0.74-0.80) next
49	# to price_score's near-unit range, so the router's behavior barely changes past
50	# w_price~0.15 -- 0.1 sits in the part of that range where it still meaningfully listens
51	# to performance_score while beating the incumbent-only baseline on cost, rather than
52	# collapsing to the same picks as always-cheapest (w=1.0) or drifting into "quality-only"
53	# territory that can cost more than doing nothing (w<0.05).
54	
55	
56	def find_export(arg: str | None) -> Path:
57	    """Resolve the trajectories file/dir. Prefers `export/*.jsonl` (README §3);
58	    falls back to `data/*.jsonl` for the README's originally-documented path."""
59	    if arg:
60	        path = Path(arg)
61	        if path.is_file():
62	            return path
63	        candidates = sorted(path.glob("*.jsonl"))
64	        if candidates:
65	            return candidates[0]
66	        sys.exit(f"no *.jsonl found in {path}")
67	    for directory in (Path("export"), Path("data")):
68	        candidates = sorted(directory.glob("*.jsonl"))
69	        if candidates:
70	            return candidates[0]
71	    sys.exit("no export found — pass a path, or place a chunk under export/ or data/")
72	
73	
74	def score_trajectory(trajectory, base_models: list[ModelLLM]) -> dict:
75	    """Run both scoring stages on a fresh copy of the pool, then read off each
76	    policy's cost for this trajectory's next call.
77	
78	    Both scoring stages run regardless -- the router's pick at DEFAULT_WEIGHT depends
79	    on performance_score even though this script only reports cost.
80	    """
81	    models = [m.model_copy(deep=True) for m in base_models]
82	    score_price(trajectory, models)
83	    score_performance(trajectory, models)
84	    costs = estimate_costs(trajectory, models)
85	
86	    served = trajectory.served_model
87	    random_cost = sum(costs.values()) / len(models)
88	
89	    model_stage.aggregate_scores(
90	        models, w_price=DEFAULT_WEIGHT, w_performance=round(1 - DEFAULT_WEIGHT, 2)
91	    )
92	    decision = model_stage.decide(trajectory, models)
93	
94	    return {
95	        "id": trajectory.id,
96	        "served_model": served,
97	        "total_calls": trajectory.total_calls,
98	        "strongest_cost": costs[STRONGEST_NAME],
99	        "cheapest_cost": costs[CHEAPEST_NAME],
100	        "incumbent_cost": costs[served],
101	        "random_cost": random_cost,
102	        "router_cost": costs[decision.top_model],
103	        "router_decision": decision.label,
104	    }
105	
106	
107	def main() -> None:
108	    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
109	    parser.add_argument("export", nargs="?", default=None, help="export dir or .jsonl file")
110	    parser.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=None, help="only score the first N trajectories")
111	    args = parser.parse_args()
112	
113	    export_path = find_export(args.export)
114	    base_models = build_model_list()
115	    print(f"reading {export_path} ...")
116	
117	    results = []
118	    for i, trajectory in enumerate(analyze_file(export_path)):
119	        if args.limit and i >= args.limit:
120	            break
121	        results.append(score_trajectory(trajectory, base_models))
122	        if (i + 1) % 200 == 0:
123	            print(f"  scored {i + 1} trajectories...")
124	
125	    n = len(results)
126	    print(f"scored {n} trajectories\n")
127	
128	    results_dir = Path("results")
129	    results_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
130	
131	    write_per_trajectory_csv(results_dir / "benchmark_trajectories.csv", results)
132	    print_summary(results, n)
133	    plot_total_cost(results_dir / "total_cost.png", results)
134	
135	
136	def write_per_trajectory_csv(path: Path, results: list[dict]) -> None:
137	    """Headline per-trajectory table at DEFAULT_WEIGHT, for a quick eyeball diff.
138	    Covers every trajectory in the export."""
139	    with open(path, "w", newline="") as handle:
140	        writer = csv.writer(handle)
141	        writer.writerow([
142	            "id", "served_model", "total_calls",
143	            "strongest_cost_usd", "cheapest_cost_usd", "incumbent_cost_usd",
144	            "router_cost_usd", "router_decision",
145	        ])
146	        for row in results:
147	            writer.writerow([
148	                row["id"], row["served_model"], row["total_calls"],
149	                f"{row['strongest_cost']:.6f}", f"{row['cheapest_cost']:.6f}",
150	                f"{row['incumbent_cost']:.6f}", f"{row['router_cost']:.6f}", row["router_decision"],
151	            ])
152	    print(f"wrote {path}")
153	
154	
155	def print_summary(results: list[dict], n: int) -> None:
156	    strongest_cost = sum(r["strongest_cost"] for r in results) / n
157	    incumbent_cost = sum(r["incumbent_cost"] for r in results) / n
158	    router_cost = sum(r["router_cost"] for r in results) / n
159	    hold_rate = sum(1 for r in results if r["router_decision"] == "HOLD") / n
160	
161	    print(f"--- summary over all {n} trajectories (next-call cost, USD) ---")
162	    print(f"  incumbent-only (observed policy, today, always HOLD): ${incumbent_cost:.6f} avg/trajectory")
163	    print(f"  always-strongest (claude-fable-5):                     ${strongest_cost:.6f} avg/trajectory")
164	    print(f"  router @ w_price={DEFAULT_WEIGHT}:                                   ${router_cost:.6f} avg/trajectory "
165	          f"({hold_rate:.0%} HOLD)")
166	    print(f"  router savings vs incumbent-only:   {100 * (1 - router_cost / incumbent_cost):.1f}%")
167	    print(f"  router savings vs always-strongest: {100 * (1 - router_cost / strongest_cost):.1f}%")
168	    print()
169	    print("NOTE: cost figures are real estimates from price_model.py's cache-aware formula (still "
170	          "estimates: no `usage` field in the export, tokens are tiktoken-counted, see README §5). "
171	          "The router's picks still depend on performance_score (router_models/performance_model.py, "
172	          "a fitted pairwise-conformity proxy, not measured ground truth) even though this summary "
173	          "only reports cost.")
174	
175	
176	def plot_total_cost(path: Path, results: list[dict]) -> None:
177	    """Bar chart: total estimated USD across every trajectory's next call, one bar per
178	    policy -- no quality axis, just the real cache-aware cost formula summed over the
179	    export.
180	    """
181	    import matplotlib
182	    matplotlib.use("Agg")
183	    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
184	
185	    bars = [
186	        ("random\nrouting", sum(r["random_cost"] for r in results), "#FFFFFF", "#6748FD"),
187	        ("always-\ncheapest", sum(r["cheapest_cost"] for r in results), "#FFFFFF", "#150079"),
188	        ("always-\nstrongest", sum(r["strongest_cost"] for r in results), "#FFBD9E", "#150079"),
189	        ("always\nhold", sum(r["incumbent_cost"] for r in results), "#150079", "#150079"),
190	        (f"router\n(w={DEFAULT_WEIGHT})", sum(r["router_cost"] for r in results), "#6748FD", "#6748FD"),
191	    ]
192	    bars.sort(key=lambda b: b[1])
193	
194	    labels = [b[0] for b in bars]
195	    totals = [b[1] for b in bars]
196	    face_colors = [b[2] for b in bars]
197	    edge_colors = [b[3] for b in bars]
198	
199	    # Log scale: totals span ~50x (the whole point of the chart is that spread), so a
200	    # linear axis squashes the four cheaper bars into an unreadable sliver at the
201	    # bottom next to always-strongest. A floor of $1 keeps every bar's base finite
202	    # (log(0) is undefined) without hiding how small the cheap bars really are --
203	    # exact dollar amounts are annotated on every bar regardless of the axis scale.
204	    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
205	    x = range(len(bars))
206	    ax.bar(x, totals, color=face_colors, edgecolor=edge_colors, linewidth=1.5, width=0.62, bottom=1)
207	    ax.set_yscale("log")
208	    ax.set_ylim(1, max(totals) * 2.2)
209	
210	    for i, total in enumerate(totals):
211	        ax.annotate(f"${total:,.2f}", (i, total), textcoords="offset points",
212	                    xytext=(0, 12), ha="center", fontsize=9.5, color="#150079")
213	
214	    ax.set_xticks(list(x))
215	    ax.set_xticklabels(labels, fontsize=9.5)
216	    ax.set_ylabel(f"total estimated cost, next call across {len(results)} trajectories (USD, log scale)")
217	    ax.set_title("Total cost by policy")
218	    fig.text(0.01, 0.01,
219	              "cost is a real estimate (price_model.py's cache-aware formula); router uses a fitted-proxy\n"
220	              "performance_score (performance_model.py); always-cheapest = gpt-5.6-luna, "
221	              "always-strongest = claude-fable-5",
222	              fontsize=7, color="#666666")
223	    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.05, 1, 1))
224	    fig.savefig(path, dpi=150)
225	    print(f"wrote {path}")
226

**Benchmark results** (1,000 real trajectories, `export/trajectories_v1_01.jsonl`):

| Policy | Avg cost/trajectory |
|---|---|
| always-strongest (`claude-fable-5`) | $0.296590 |
| incumbent-only (today's always-HOLD) | $0.027676 |
| **router (w_price=0.1)** | **$0.010206** (2% HOLD rate) |

Router saves **63.1%** vs. today's production policy and **96.6%** vs. always routing to the strongest model, while still consulting `performance_score` (not price alone). Full per-trajectory breakdown is in the CSV; the bar chart is log-scaled since costs span ~50x across policies.
