1	"""Assign `price_score` to each candidate `ModelLLM` for one `Trajectory`.
2	
3	Per the README's scoring contract (§5): `price_score` is `[0, 1]`, higher = cheaper,
4	normalized *within this trajectory's candidate pool* — not against some global price
5	scale. This module is a pure function of `(Trajectory, List[ModelLLM])`; the only place
6	it reads `Trajectory.served_model` is the switching-cost check below, which the README
7	explicitly carves out as legitimate (it is not a task-quality proxy).
8	
9	The crux, per docs/FULL_REPORT.md §5: providers cache the shared input prefix across a trajectory's
10	calls, and a model switch resets that cache. So "cheaper per token" and "cheaper for
11	the next call" are different questions once a trajectory has accumulated context — a
12	model switch pays full uncached price for the whole next prompt, which in long
13	trajectories can dwarf any per-token saving. That's the entire reason this module needs
14	`served_model` at all: to tell a HOLD's mostly-cached next call apart from a CHANGE's
15	fully-uncached one.
16	
17	The base for "how big is the next prompt" is `Trajectory.last_call_input_tokens`, not
18	`total_tokens` -- see `_next_call_tokens` for why: every call resends the whole history
19	up to that point, so the next call's size tracks the size of the *most recent* call, not
20	the sum of every past call's own (already-superseded) full-history snapshot.
21	"""
22	
23	from __future__ import annotations
24	
25	from cheapy.models.llm import ModelLLM
26	from cheapy.models.trajectory import Trajectory
27	
28	
29	def _next_call_tokens(trajectory: Trajectory) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
30	    """ESTIMATE the shape of the trajectory's next call.
31	
32	    Returns (last_call_input_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens).
33	
34	    `last_call_input_tokens` is `Trajectory.last_call_input_tokens` taken at face value:
35	    the size of the most recently recovered call's full prompt (tool schemas + history
36	    up to that point). Because every call resends the whole history, this is the best
37	    available proxy for the size of the *next* call's prompt.
38	
39	    This deliberately does NOT use `total_tokens`. `total_tokens` sums every past call's
40	    prompt -- each of which was itself a full-history resend at the time -- so it adds up
41	    several superseded snapshots of a growing thing instead of reporting the size of the
42	    latest one. On a trajectory whose prompt grows roughly linearly over `n` calls,
43	    `total_tokens` overstates the real next-call size by very roughly a factor of `n/2`,
44	    and can trip the context-window feasibility gate below for a model that would
45	    actually serve the real next call fine. `last_call_input_tokens` doesn't have that
46	    problem: it's one call's real size, not an accumulating sum.
47	
48	    `increment_tokens` approximates how much *new* content (tool outputs, replies, ...)
49	    a typical call in this trajectory appends, as the trajectory's own average per-call
50	    growth (`last_call_input_tokens / total_calls`) -- not `total_tokens / total_calls`,
51	    which is the same superseded-snapshots mistake `last_call_input_tokens` exists to
52	    avoid, just applied to the increment instead of the prompt size: it averages in
53	    every past call's own (smaller, since-outgrown) prompt size, not how much this
54	    trajectory actually grows per step. There is no better signal available for the
55	    increment itself: the next call's actual new content is by definition not in the
56	    log yet. This average is a separate, smaller known simplification (it can over- or
57	    under-estimate a single step depending on whether the trajectory's growth is
58	    front- or back-loaded) -- see the README's "Known simplifications".
59	    """
60	    last_call_input_tokens = float(trajectory.last_call_input_tokens)
61	    increment_tokens = (
62	        last_call_input_tokens / trajectory.total_calls if trajectory.total_calls else 0.0
63	    )
64	    next_output_tokens = trajectory.avg_output_tokens_per_call
65	    return last_call_input_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens
66	
67	
68	def _next_call_cost(trajectory: Trajectory, model: ModelLLM) -> float:
69	    """ESTIMATE the USD cost of `model` serving this trajectory's next call.
70	
71	    No candidate is ever excluded for having too small a context window. If
72	    `last_call_input_tokens` is bigger than what `model` can hold, this assumes the
73	    context gets compacted down to the model's max `context_window_size` before the
74	    call is sent -- clamp the size, then price it with the exact same cache-aware
75	    formula used for every other call, holding or switching alike.
76	    """
77	    last_call_input_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens = _next_call_tokens(
78	        trajectory
79	    )
80	    last_call_input_tokens = min(last_call_input_tokens, float(model.context_window_size))
81	    next_input_tokens = last_call_input_tokens + increment_tokens
82	
83	    holding = model.name == trajectory.served_model
84	    if holding:
85	        # Same model as the log: the last call's whole prompt was already sent once and
86	        # is cache-eligible; only the new increment is guaranteed uncached. Cap at
87	        # `last_call_input_tokens` -- `total_cached_tokens` is a whole-trajectory
88	        # aggregate and can exceed the size of any single call, but only that much of it
89	        # is actually part of *this* call's bill.
90	        cached_tokens = min(float(trajectory.total_cached_tokens), last_call_input_tokens)
91	        uncached_tokens = (last_call_input_tokens - cached_tokens) + increment_tokens
92	    else:
93	        # A switch resets the provider's prefix cache: the whole next prompt is
94	        # uncached, not just the increment. This is the cache trap from docs/FULL_REPORT.md §5.
95	        cached_tokens = 0.0
96	        uncached_tokens = next_input_tokens
97	
98	    input_cost = (
99	        uncached_tokens * model.input_price_per_1m
100	        + cached_tokens * model.cached_input_price_per_1m
101	    ) / 1_000_000
102	    output_cost = next_output_tokens * model.output_price_per_1m / 1_000_000
103	    return input_cost + output_cost
104	
105	
106	def estimate_costs(trajectory: Trajectory, models: list[ModelLLM]) -> dict[str, float]:
107	    """ESTIMATE the USD cost of each candidate in `models` serving the trajectory's next
108	    call, keyed by model name — see `_next_call_cost`.
109	
110	    Public so callers other than `score_price` -- e.g. a benchmark comparing policies by
111	    actual dollar cost rather than the normalized `price_score` -- can get the same
112	    per-candidate cost figures `score_price` normalizes, without duplicating the
113	    cache-trap cost logic in `_next_call_cost`.
114	    """
115	    return {model.name: _next_call_cost(trajectory, model) for model in models}
116	
117	
118	def score_price(trajectory: Trajectory, models: list[ModelLLM]) -> list[ModelLLM]:
119	    """Enrich each `ModelLLM` in `models` with a `price_score` in `(0, 1]`.
120	
121	    Higher is cheaper. Costs are estimated per `_next_call_cost` (via `estimate_costs`)
122	    and scored as a ratio to the *cheapest* candidate in this trajectory's candidate
123	    pool — per docs/FULL_REPORT.md §5's "normalize within the candidate pool, not globally" — rather
124	    than min-max stretched across the pool's full price range. A candidate priced at `k`
125	    times the cheapest one scores `1/k`: a candidate only marginally above the cheapest
126	    price lands close to `1.0`, not at the same `0.0` floor a wildly pricier candidate
127	    would get under min-max. It also depends only on the cheapest cost, not the
128	    priciest, so a candidate's score no longer shifts just because some unrelated,
129	    pricier (or cheaper) candidate joins the pool. Every candidate gets a real cost (a
130	    too-small context window is compacted to fit, never excluded — see
131	    `_next_call_cost`), so every model in the pool gets a ratio-based score.
132	    """
133	    costs = estimate_costs(trajectory, models)
134	    cheapest = min(costs.values())
135	
136	    for model in models:
137	        cost = costs[model.name]
138	        # cost == 0 only when cheapest == 0 too (costs are never negative), so this is
139	        # the tie-at-the-top case, not a magic number -- 0/0 is otherwise undefined.
140	        model.price_score = 1.0 if cost == 0 else cheapest / cost
141	
142	    return models

1	"""`performance_model.py` — sets `ModelLLM.performance_score`, per docs/FULL_REPORT.md §2/§5.
2	
3	Thin adapter only. All the scoring logic — pairwise divergence, prior-weighted
4	conformity, the ridge regressor — lives in `research/capability_fitting/`, whose design is
5	recorded in `docs/capability_model.md`. This module exists
6	solely to satisfy the stage contract every `src/cheapy/routing/` file follows: a function of
7	`(Trajectory, list[ModelLLM]) -> list[ModelLLM]` that enriches the given `ModelLLM`
8	objects in place (docs/FULL_REPORT.md §2, "The scoring chain").
9	
10	Never reads `trajectory.served_model` (docs/FULL_REPORT.md §5's "Shared contract") — neither this
11	module nor `capability_model.score_for_trajectory` touches it for scoring; it is read
12	only inside `research/capability_fitting/` as an explicit, logged diagnostic (spec §1.0,
13	§8), never as a feature.
14	"""
15	
16	from __future__ import annotations
17	
18	from cheapy.capability.capability_model import DEFAULT_BETA, score_for_trajectory
19	from cheapy.models.llm import ModelLLM
20	from cheapy.models.trajectory import Trajectory
21	
22	#: Default conformity weighting (spec §4) — `w_i = prior_i ** BETA`, so BETA sets how much
23	#: more a high-prior model's agreement counts than a low-prior model's.
24	#:
25	#: **3.0, not 1.0.** The design has two intents, and only one of them holds at BETA = 1.
26	#: Measured over 200 trajectories (`research/capability_fitting/` sweep):
27	#:
28	#:   (1) unanimity compresses scores toward 1 — holds at every BETA (spread on settled
29	#:       steps is ~half that on contested ones, and nothing falls below ~0.80).
30	#:   (2) divergence rewards conformity with the *most intelligent* model — fails at
31	#:       BETA = 1: rank correlation between the score ordering and `BASE_CAPABILITY` is
32	#:       only 0.52 on contested steps, and the model rewarded is `gpt-5.6-sol`, a
33	#:       mid-prior GPT that wins by sitting at the centre of an all-GPT probe panel.
34	#:
35	#: rho(score, prior) on contested steps by BETA: 0.20 (0.0), 0.52 (1.0), 0.70 (2.0),
36	#: 0.73 (3.0), 0.75 (5.0). BETA = 3 is the lowest value at which the highest-prior model
37	#: actually tops the ranking on contested steps, so it is the cheapest point that
38	#: satisfies intent (2) without flattening the score into the prior — rho keeps creeping
39	#: up past 3, but only by letting the prior dominate the measurement.
40	#:
41	#: Callers sweeping the cost/capability trade-off pass their own value straight through.
42	#: The value itself lives in `capability_model` and is imported, not restated, so the
43	#: two call sites cannot drift apart.
44	__all__ = ["DEFAULT_BETA", "score_performance"]
45	
46	
47	def score_performance(
48	    trajectory: Trajectory, models: list[ModelLLM], beta: float = DEFAULT_BETA
49	) -> list[ModelLLM]:
50	    """Set `performance_score` on every `ModelLLM` in `models` that is in the trained
51	    candidate set (spec §1.0's seven), leaving the rest at `None` — never `0` (see
52	    `ModelLLM.performance_score`'s docstring: unset must not be treated as worst-possible
53	    in any downstream trade-off).
54	    """
55	    return score_for_trajectory(trajectory, models, beta=beta)
56

1	"""`router.py` — the last stage: weighted aggregation, ranking, HOLD / CHANGE TO.
2	
3	Per docs/FULL_REPORT.md §2 this stage takes the `ModelLLM` objects the two scoring stages already
4	enriched and combines their scores into one number::
5	
6	    final_score = (W_COST · price_score + W_PERFORMANCE · performance_score)
7	                  / (W_COST + W_PERFORMANCE)
8	
9	The division is what keeps `final_score` inside `[0, 1]` alongside its two inputs, so
10	weights can be passed as any pair of non-negative numbers (`0.7 / 0.3`, `7 / 3`, `1 / 0`)
11	without changing the scale the ranking is read on.
12	
13	**Weights are arguments, never module constants** (docs/FULL_REPORT.md §5, "Aggregation"): sweeping
14	them is how the cost/quality frontier gets produced, so `aggregate_scores` and `route`
15	require them explicitly rather than defaulting to one operating point. The only default
16	here is `min_gain`, which is a switching threshold, not an operating point.
17	
18	`served_model` is read exactly once, in `decide`, to compare the winner against the
19	incumbent — that is the decision itself, not a scoring feature. The scores it ranks were
20	produced without it (`performance_model`), or with the one switching-cost carve-out
21	docs/FULL_REPORT.md §5 grants (`price_model`).
22	"""
23	
24	from __future__ import annotations
25	
26	from dataclasses import dataclass
27	from typing import Literal
28	
29	from cheapy.models.llm import ModelLLM
30	from cheapy.models.trajectory import Trajectory
31	from cheapy.routing.performance_model import DEFAULT_BETA, score_performance
32	from cheapy.routing.price_model import score_price
33	
34	__all__ = ["ScoreRow", "RoutingDecision", "aggregate_scores", "rank", "decide", "route"]
35	
36	Action = Literal["HOLD", "CHANGE"]
37	
38	
39	@dataclass(frozen=True)
40	class ScoreRow:
41	    """One candidate's line on a trajectory's scoreboard.
42	
43	    A flat snapshot taken at `decide` time, because the `ModelLLM` objects it comes from
44	    are rebuilt and re-scored for the next trajectory — holding on to them would hand a
45	    later reader the wrong trajectory's numbers.
46	    """
47	
48	    name: str
49	    final_score: float
50	    price_score: float
51	    performance_score: float
52	    is_served: bool
53	    """True for the model that actually served this trajectory (the incumbent)."""
54	
55	
56	@dataclass(frozen=True)
57	class RoutingDecision:
58	    """What the router concluded for one trajectory's next call."""
59	
60	    trajectory_id: int
61	    served_model: str
62	    top_model: str
63	    action: Action
64	    label: str
65	    """`"HOLD"` or `"CHANGE TO <model>"` — the docs/FULL_REPORT.md §1 verdict string."""
66	
67	    top_final_score: float
68	    top_price_score: float
69	    top_performance_score: float
70	    served_final_score: float | None
71	    """`None` when the incumbent was not in the candidate pool, or went unscored."""
72	    score_gap: float
73	    """`top_final_score - served_final_score`; `0.0` when the incumbent is the winner.
74	
75	    Also the "how much does this decision matter here" signal: a gap near zero means any
76	    candidate would do and the choice is nearly free either way."""
77	
78	    scoreboard: tuple[ScoreRow, ...]
79	    """Every scored candidate, best first, with the two inputs behind each `final_score`.
80	
81	    This is what `--verbose` prints. It is kept on the decision rather than recomputed by
82	    the caller so the printed board is, by construction, the board the verdict came from.
83	    """
84	    unscored: tuple[str, ...]
85	    """Candidates left out of the ranking because a stage did not score them."""
86	
87	    @property
88	    def ranking(self) -> tuple[str, ...]:
89	        """Every scored candidate by name, best first."""
90	        return tuple(row.name for row in self.scoreboard)
91	
92	
93	def aggregate_scores(
94	    models: list[ModelLLM], *, w_cost: float, w_performance: float
95	) -> list[ModelLLM]:
96	    """Set `final_score` in place on every fully-scored `ModelLLM` and return `models`.
97	
98	    A model missing either input keeps `final_score = None`. It is **not** scored on the
99	    half it has: an unset score means "this stage did not score this model", and both
100	    `ModelLLM` docstrings are explicit that it must never be read as 0 — doing so would
101	    rank an unscored model as the worst possible one and quietly drop it out of
102	    contention on evidence that was never gathered.
103	    """
104	    if w_cost < 0 or w_performance < 0:
105	        raise ValueError(f"weights must be >= 0, got {w_cost} / {w_performance}")
106	    total = w_cost + w_performance
107	    if total == 0:
108	        raise ValueError("w_cost + w_performance must be > 0 — no ranking is defined at 0/0")
109	
110	    for model in models:
111	        if model.price_score is None or model.performance_score is None:
112	            model.final_score = None
113	            continue
114	        model.final_score = (
115	            w_cost * model.price_score + w_performance * model.performance_score
116	        ) / total
117	    return models
118	
119	
120	def rank(models: list[ModelLLM], served_model: str | None = None) -> list[ModelLLM]:
121	    """Scored candidates, best `final_score` first.
122	
123	    Ties break toward `served_model` and then by name. Both tie-breaks exist to make the
124	    ranking deterministic, and the first also keeps a dead-even score from reading as a
125	    reason to switch: switching has costs the score does not fully capture (the reset
126	    prefix cache is only the measurable one), so an exact tie resolves to the incumbent.
127	    """
128	    scored = [model for model in models if model.final_score is not None]
129	    return sorted(
130	        scored,
131	        key=lambda m: (-m.final_score, m.name != served_model, m.name),  # type: ignore[operator]
132	    )
133	
134	
135	def decide(
136	    trajectory: Trajectory, models: list[ModelLLM], *, min_gain: float = 0.0
137	) -> RoutingDecision:
138	    """Rank the already-aggregated `models` and emit the HOLD / CHANGE TO verdict.
139	
140	    `min_gain` is the `final_score` improvement a challenger must show over the incumbent
141	    before the switch is worth making — a deadband, not a scoring weight. At the default
142	    `0.0` any improvement at all flips the decision to CHANGE; raise it to suppress
143	    switches whose predicted gain is inside the noise of an estimate built on estimated
144	    tokens and predicted agreement.
145	    """
146	    if min_gain < 0:
147	        raise ValueError(f"min_gain must be >= 0, got {min_gain}")
148	
149	    ranked = rank(models, trajectory.served_model)
150	    if not ranked:
151	        raise ValueError(
152	            f"trajectory {trajectory.id}: no candidate has both a price_score and a "
153	            "performance_score — run score_price and score_performance first"
154	        )
155	
156	    top = ranked[0]
157	    served = next(
158	        (m for m in ranked if m.name == trajectory.served_model), None
159	    )
160	    served_final = served.final_score if served is not None else None
161	
162	    # An unranked incumbent leaves no baseline to beat, so the ranking's own winner
163	    # stands: gain is undefined, not zero, and min_gain cannot be applied to it.
164	    gain = top.final_score - served_final if served_final is not None else None  # type: ignore[operator]
165	    holds = top.name == trajectory.served_model or (gain is not None and gain <= min_gain)
166	
167	    if holds and served is not None:
168	        top = served
169	
170	    return RoutingDecision(
171	        trajectory_id=trajectory.id,
172	        served_model=trajectory.served_model,
173	        top_model=top.name,
174	        action="HOLD" if holds else "CHANGE",
175	        label="HOLD" if holds else f"CHANGE TO {top.name}",
176	        top_final_score=top.final_score,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
177	        top_price_score=top.price_score,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
178	        top_performance_score=top.performance_score,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
179	        served_final_score=served_final,
180	        score_gap=0.0 if holds else gain if gain is not None else 0.0,
181	        scoreboard=tuple(
182	            ScoreRow(
183	                name=m.name,
184	                final_score=m.final_score,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
185	                price_score=m.price_score,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
186	                performance_score=m.performance_score,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
187	                is_served=m.name == trajectory.served_model,
188	            )
189	            for m in ranked
190	        ),
191	        unscored=tuple(m.name for m in models if m.final_score is None),
192	    )
193	
194	
195	def route(
196	    trajectory: Trajectory,
197	    models: list[ModelLLM],
198	    *,
199	    w_cost: float,
200	    w_performance: float,
201	    beta: float = DEFAULT_BETA,
202	    min_gain: float = 0.0,
203	) -> RoutingDecision:
204	    """The whole scoring chain for one trajectory, in docs/FULL_REPORT.md §2's order.
205	
206	    price -> performance -> aggregate -> decide, each stage enriching the same `models`
207	    in place. `models` must be this trajectory's own list: the stages mutate the objects,
208	    so a list shared between trajectories would carry the previous one's scores.
209	    """
210	    score_price(trajectory, models)
211	    score_performance(trajectory, models, beta=beta)
212	    aggregate_scores(models, w_cost=w_cost, w_performance=w_performance)
213	    return decide(trajectory, models, min_gain=min_gain)

Grounding this in what's actually in `docs/FULL_REPORT.md` §7 and the current code: even after the recent fix (price is now `cheapest/cost` ratio, not min-max), price_score still spans up to ~50x within the pool (`gpt-5.6-luna` vs `claude-fable-5`), while performance_score is *designed* to compress toward the top when models agree ("nothing falls below ~0.80" on settled steps, ~0.17 spread even on contested ones). A linear weighted average can't reconcile those — whichever term has more numeric spread mechanically wins, which is exactly why price saturates at `w_cost=0.15` and everything above that gives the identical all-`luna` split.

Three ways to fix it, in order of how much I'd trust each:

1. **Compress price_score's dynamic range before combining** (e.g. `(cheapest/cost)^p` for some `p < 1`, or a log-based transform) — same family of change as the ratio-to-cheapest fix already applied, touches only `price_model.py`, and doesn't go near `performance_score`, so the "agreement → narrow spread" property you want to preserve is untouched by construction. Needs one parameter picked and justified via a sweep, the same way `β=3` was justified for the capability model — this is the piece I'd actually implement first.

2. **Switch the aggregation from arithmetic to geometric mean** (`final_score = price_score^w_cost · performance_score^w_perf`). Mathematically similar effect to #1 (multiplying in log-space naturally tempers price's huge ratios) but it's a bigger interface change to `router.py`'s contract and changes what "50/50" intuitively means — I'd only reach for this if #1's single exponent turns out not to be expressive enough.

3. **Quality-tolerance gating**: treat any candidate within some delta of the best `performance_score` as tied, and break ties on price alone (a lexicographic rule, closer in spirit to how `min_gain` already works as a switching deadband). This is the option that *directly* encodes "don't penalize similar answers" instead of relying on it as a side effect of score compression — but it's a bigger structural change (two-stage decision, not one weighted number) and adds another threshold to defend.

**What I'd avoid:** stretching `performance_score`'s range to match price's (min-max normalizing it per trajectory the way price used to be). That's the obvious-looking fix, but it works directly against the thing you said you want to protect — a settled step where every model agrees would get artificially fanned back out into big score gaps between models that are functionally tied.

I'd start with #1 — smallest change, keeps the existing architecture, and is a straightforward sweep (same shape as the `w_cost` and `β` sweeps already in §7) to pick the exponent. Want me to implement that and run the sweep, or talk through #3 more first?

content.text:
The current formula (`src/cheapy/routing/price_model.py`) computes `price_score = cheapest_cost / this_model's_cost` — cheapest candidate always lands at exactly `1.0`, everyone else gets a fraction below it. The problem isn't the ratio itself, it's that the *raw* ratio still spans the full price spread of the pool. Using this project's real per-1M-token prices (ignoring caching for a moment, since input dominates output ~130:1 per the report):

| model | $/1M input | ratio score (today) |
|---|---|---|
| gpt-5.6-luna | 0.20 | **1.0000** |
| claude-sonnet-5 / gpt-5.6-terra | 2.00 | 0.1000 |
| claude-opus-5/4-8/4-6 | 5.00 | 0.0400 |
| claude-fable-5 | 10.00 | **0.0200** |

That's a 50x spread end to end (1.0 → 0.02), against performance_score's ~0.17 spread even on contested steps. The fix: raise that ratio to a fixed exponent `p ∈ (0, 1)` before it goes into the weighted average — `price_score = (cheapest_cost / cost) ** p`. Same table at `p = 0.3`:

| model | ratio score | `^0.3` |
|---|---|---|
| gpt-5.6-luna | 1.0000 | **1.0000** |
| claude-sonnet-5 | 0.1000 | 0.5012 |
| claude-opus-5 | 0.0400 | 0.3807 |
| claude-fable-5 | 0.0200 | **0.3092** |

Now the spread end to end is 1.0 → 0.31 (~3.2x) instead of 1.0 → 0.02 (50x) — the same order of magnitude as performance_score's spread, so a weighted average of the two actually blends them across a useful range of `w_cost` instead of saturating almost immediately.

Why exponentiation specifically, not some other squashing function: it's a strict generalization of what's already there, not a redesign.
- `p = 1` reproduces today's formula exactly — nothing breaks, it's additive to the existing code.
- The cheapest candidate still always scores exactly `1.0` for any `p` (since `1^p = 1`), so the "anchor point" behavior is unchanged.
- It still depends only on `cheapest_cost`, never on the priciest candidate — unlike a log-based min-max, which would reintroduce dependence on whoever happens to be priciest in *this* pool (breaking the property the current docstring explicitly calls out: "a candidate's score no longer shifts just because some unrelated, pricier or cheaper candidate joins the pool").
- It touches only `price_model.py`. `performance_score` and its agreement-compresses-the-field behavior aren't touched at all, so the "don't over-penalize similar answers" property stays exactly as designed.

Picking `p` is the real work — same shape of problem as picking `β = 3` for the capability model: run the §7-style weight sweep at a few candidate `p` values (e.g. 1.0, 0.5, 0.3, 0.15) and look for the value where the "interesting" crossover band (today, `w_cost ∈ [0.05, 0.08]`, collapsing almost immediately into saturation at 0.15) widens into something a real operator could actually dial across, rather than picking `p` by feel.

One thing to flag honestly: this makes the router *less* price-sensitive at the cheap end by design — a 50x-cheaper model no longer gets rewarded 50x, it gets rewarded `50^p`x. That's the intended fix, but it's worth stating plainly since it's a real behavior change, not just a bug fix.

Sorry — let me back up and be clearer.

There are two separate scores per model, and I'm only proposing to change **one** of them:

- **`price_score`** — how cheap a model is for the next call, 0 to 1, computed in `price_model.py`.
- **`performance_score`** — how good/capable a model is, 0 to 1, computed in `performance_model.py` (this is a *different* thing from `quality_base_value.py`, which is just a fallback prior fed into that computation, not touched by anything here).

These two get averaged into one `final_score` that decides which model wins. **The problem:** across the 9 models, `price_score` swings all the way from 1.0 down to 0.02 (the cheapest model vs. the priciest one), while `performance_score` barely moves — it stays roughly between 0.80 and 0.97 no matter which model you look at. When you average a number that swings wildly with a number that barely moves, the wildly-swinging one decides the outcome almost regardless of how you weight them. That's why the router basically always ends up picking the cheapest model.

**What I'm proposing to change:** only the `price_score` formula. Not `performance_score`. Not the quality/leaderboard data. Just the math that turns "this model's cost" into a number between 0 and 1.

Right now: `price_score = cheapest_cost / this_model's_cost`. For `claude-fable-5`, which costs 50x more than the cheapest model, that gives `1/50 = 0.02`.

The change: take that same ratio and raise it to a small power (like 0.3) before using it: `price_score = (cheapest_cost / this_model's_cost) ^ 0.3`. That turns `0.02` into `0.31` instead — still lower than the cheapest model's `1.0`, so cheap models still win when prices really matter, but the *gap* between cheapest and priciest shrinks from 50x down to about 3x, which is now roughly the same size as `performance_score`'s natural gap. So when you average the two, `performance_score` actually gets to matter instead of being drowned out.

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""Routing simulation — replays every logged trajectory through the router.
3	
4	For each JSONL line of the dataset: parse it into a `Trajectory`, build a
5	fresh candidate pool, run the docs/FULL_REPORT.md §2 scoring chain (price -> performance ->
6	weighted final score), and record the verdict — HOLD, or CHANGE TO <model>.
7	
8	Writes one row per trajectory to `routing_simul.csv` beside the dataset and prints a short
9	overview. Nothing is written between stages: the simulation is one pass and the CSV
10	is its only artifact.
11	
12	Settings come from `cheapy.yaml` at the repo root (W_COST, W_PERFORMANCE, BETA,
13	CACHE_HIT_RATE, VERBOSE); every one of them has a flag here that wins for a single run.
14	
15	Every token figure behind these decisions is an ESTIMATE (no `usage` field in the
16	export — see docs/FULL_REPORT.md §5), so the costs and savings reported here are estimates too.
17	
18	    ./run_simul.sh                                  # data/, cheapy.yaml settings
19	    ./run_simul.sh path/to/export.jsonl             # any dataset, CSV written beside it
20	    ./run_simul.sh --w-cost 0.7 --w-performance 0.3
21	    ./run_simul.sh --limit 5 --verbose              # per-trajectory scoreboards
22	    ./run_simul.sh --limit 50 --min-gain 0.02
23	"""
24	
25	from __future__ import annotations
26	
27	import argparse
28	import csv
29	import sys
30	from collections import Counter
31	from pathlib import Path
32	
33	SRC_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]        # src/
34	REPO_ROOT = SRC_ROOT.parent                           # repo root
35	if str(SRC_ROOT) not in sys.path:  # allow `python src/cheapy/cli.py` as well as `-m cheapy.cli`
36	    sys.path.insert(0, str(SRC_ROOT))
37	
38	from cheapy.config import SimulationConfig, load_config  # noqa: E402
39	from cheapy.models.llm import ModelLLM  # noqa: E402
40	from cheapy.models.trajectory import Trajectory  # noqa: E402
41	from cheapy.preprocessing.model_list import build_model_list  # noqa: E402
42	from cheapy.preprocessing.trajectory_analyzer import analyze  # noqa: E402
43	from cheapy.routing.router import RoutingDecision, route  # noqa: E402
44	
45	DEFAULT_DATA_DIR = REPO_ROOT / "data"
46	OUTPUT_NAME = "routing_simul.csv"
47	
48	_CSV_COLUMNS = (
49	    "trajectory_id",
50	    "source_chunk",
51	    "served_model",
52	    "decision",
53	    "top_model",
54	    "action",
55	    "top_final_score",
56	    "top_price_score",
57	    "top_performance_score",
58	    "served_final_score",
59	    "score_gap",
60	    "total_calls",
61	    "total_tokens",
62	    "ranking",
63	    "unscored",
64	)
65	
66	
67	def resolve_dataset(path: Path) -> tuple[list[Path], Path]:
68	    """`(chunks, output_dir)` for a dataset given as either a `.jsonl` file or a directory.
69	
70	    A file routes just that file and writes the CSV beside it; a directory routes every
71	    `*.jsonl` in it, sorted, and writes the CSV inside it.
72	    """
73	    if path.is_file():
74	        return [path], path.parent
75	    if path.is_dir():
76	        chunks = sorted(path.glob("*.jsonl"))
77	        if not chunks:
78	            raise SystemExit(f"no *.jsonl chunks found in {path}")
79	        return chunks, path
80	    raise SystemExit(f"dataset not found: {path}")
81	
82	
83	def iter_trajectories(chunks: list[Path], limit: int | None = None, *, cache_hit_rate: float):
84	    """Yield `(Trajectory, chunk_name)` for every JSONL line of every chunk.
85	
86	    Files are read in the order given and ids come from one counter across all of them, so
87	    an id identifies a trajectory within the run — `analyze_file` restarts at 0 per file,
88	    which would collide the moment a second chunk lands. `Trajectory` forbids extra
89	    fields, so the chunk name travels alongside rather than on the model.
90	    """
91	
92	    count = 0
93	    for chunk in chunks:
94	        with open(chunk, encoding="utf-8") as handle:
95	            for line in handle:
96	                line = line.strip()
97	                if not line:
98	                    continue
99	                if limit is not None and count >= limit:
100	                    return
101	                yield analyze(line, count, cache_hit_rate=cache_hit_rate), chunk.name
102	                count += 1
103	
104	
105	def simulate(
106	    chunks: list[Path],
107	    config: SimulationConfig,
108	    *,
109	    min_gain: float = 0.0,
110	    limit: int | None = None,
111	    on_result=None,
112	) -> list[tuple[RoutingDecision, Trajectory, str]]:
113	    """Route every trajectory in `chunks` and return the decisions.
114	
115	    A fresh `build_model_list()` per trajectory is deliberate, not wasteful: the scoring
116	    stages enrich `ModelLLM` objects in place (docs/FULL_REPORT.md §2), so a pool shared across
117	    trajectories would hand each one the previous trajectory's scores.
118	
119	    `on_result` is called with each `(decision, trajectory, chunk_name)` as it is
120	    produced — that is how `--verbose` prints a scoreboard per trajectory instead of
121	    waiting for the whole export to finish.
122	    """
123	    results: list[tuple[RoutingDecision, Trajectory, str]] = []
124	    for trajectory, chunk_name in iter_trajectories(
125	        chunks, limit=limit, cache_hit_rate=config.cache_hit_rate
126	    ):
127	        models: list[ModelLLM] = build_model_list()
128	        decision = route(
129	            trajectory,
130	            models,
131	            w_cost=config.w_cost,
132	            w_performance=config.w_performance,
133	            beta=config.beta,
134	            min_gain=min_gain,
135	        )
136	        result = (decision, trajectory, chunk_name)
137	        results.append(result)
138	        if on_result is not None:
139	            on_result(*result)
140	    return results
141	
142	
143	def write_csv(results: list[tuple[RoutingDecision, Trajectory, str]], path: Path) -> Path:
144	    """One row per routed trajectory."""
145	    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as handle:
146	        writer = csv.writer(handle)
147	        writer.writerow(_CSV_COLUMNS)
148	        for decision, trajectory, chunk_name in results:
149	            writer.writerow(
150	                (
151	                    decision.trajectory_id,
152	                    chunk_name,
153	                    decision.served_model,
154	                    decision.label,
155	                    decision.top_model,
156	                    decision.action,
157	                    f"{decision.top_final_score:.6f}",
158	                    f"{decision.top_price_score:.6f}",
159	                    f"{decision.top_performance_score:.6f}",
160	                    ""
161	                    if decision.served_final_score is None
162	                    else f"{decision.served_final_score:.6f}",
163	                    f"{decision.score_gap:.6f}",
164	                    trajectory.total_calls,
165	                    trajectory.total_tokens,
166	                    "|".join(decision.ranking),
167	                    "|".join(decision.unscored),
168	                )
169	            )
170	    return path
171	
172	
173	def print_scoreboard(decision: RoutingDecision, trajectory: Trajectory) -> None:
174	    """The full candidate ranking behind one verdict — what `--verbose` prints.
175	
176	    Every candidate the router scored, best `final_score` first, with the two numbers
177	    that produced it. The incumbent is marked `<-- served`, so a HOLD reads as "the
178	    marked row is on top" and a CHANGE reads as "these rows beat the marked one".
179	    """
180	    header = (
181	        f"  trajectory {decision.trajectory_id}  "
182	        f"({trajectory.total_calls} calls, {trajectory.total_tokens:,} est. tokens)  "
183	        f"-> {decision.label}"
184	    )
185	    print(f"\n{header}")
186	    print(f"  {'':<3} {'model':<20} {'final':>8} {'price':>8} {'perf':>8}")
187	    print(f"  {'-' * 3} {'-' * 20} {'-' * 8} {'-' * 8} {'-' * 8}")
188	    for position, row in enumerate(decision.scoreboard, start=1):
189	        marker = "  <-- served" if row.is_served else ""
190	        print(
191	            f"  {position:<3} {row.name:<20} {row.final_score:>8.4f} "
192	            f"{row.price_score:>8.4f} {row.performance_score:>8.4f}{marker}"
193	        )
194	    if decision.unscored:
195	        print(f"      unscored: {', '.join(decision.unscored)}")
196	
197	
198	def print_overview(results: list[tuple[RoutingDecision, Trajectory, str]]) -> None:
199	    """Short terminal summary: the HOLD / CHANGE split and where the changes go."""
200	    total = len(results)
201	    decisions = [decision for decision, _, _ in results]
202	    holds = sum(1 for d in decisions if d.action == "HOLD")
203	    changes = total - holds
204	    targets = Counter(d.top_model for d in decisions if d.action == "CHANGE")
205	
206	    def pct(n: int) -> str:
207	        return f"{100 * n / total:.1f}%" if total else "n/a"
208	
209	    print(f"\n  {total} trajectories routed")
210	    print(f"    HOLD       {holds:>5}  ({pct(holds)})")
211	    print(f"    CHANGE TO  {changes:>5}  ({pct(changes)})")
212	
213	    if targets:
214	        top_model, top_count = targets.most_common(1)[0]
215	        print(f"\n  most-changed-to: {top_model}  ({top_count} of {changes} changes)")
216	        for name, count in targets.most_common():
217	            print(f"    {name:<20} {count:>5}  ({pct(count)} of all trajectories)")
218

220	def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
221	    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
222	        description=__doc__.splitlines()[0],

66	    def test_partial_cache_hold_splits_context_correctly(self):
67	        # last_call_input_tokens=3,000, total_calls=5 -> increment=3,000/5=600, based on
68	        # last_call_input_tokens (not total_tokens/total_calls). HOLD should bill 1,800 at
69	        # the cached rate and (3,000-1,800)+600=1,800 at the normal rate -- based on the
70	        # size of the last actual call, not the trajectory's cumulative total_tokens.
71	        trajectory = make_trajectory(
72	            served_model="model-a",

83	        self.assertAlmostEqual(cost, expected)

102	        # increment is uncached.
103	        expected = (800 * 2.0 + 8_000 * 0.2) / 1_000_000
104	        self.assertAlmostEqual(cost, expected)

246	
247	        by_name = {m.name: m.price_score for m in models}

262	    def test_small_context_window_model_gets_real_score_not_forced_zero(self):
263	        # A model too small to hold the estimated next call unclamped is no longer
264	        # zeroed out -- it's priced on its clamped (compacted) size through the same
265	        # formula as everyone else, and can land anywhere in the ranking on its own
266	        # merits, including winning on price if billing less genuinely costs less.
267	        trajectory = make_trajectory(
268	            served_model="model-a",
269	            total_calls=5,
270	            last_call_input_tokens=3_000,
271	            total_cached_tokens=1_800,

276	            make_model("model-b"),  # switching, full context window
277	            make_model("tiny", context_window_size=1_000),  # switching, clamped

283	        # model-a (hold): cached=min(1800,3000)=1800, uncached=(3000-1800)+600=1800

287	        # Ratio-to-cheapest (tiny, 0.0032): tiny=1.0, model-a=0.0032/0.00396=80/99,
288	        # model-b=0.0032/0.0072=4/9 -- pricier than tiny, but not zeroed just for being

1	"""Simulation settings — the one place `cheapy.yaml` is read.
2	
3	The router itself takes every knob as a call argument (`route(..., w_cost=...)`); this
4	module exists so the *CLI* has a file to read defaults from instead of hardcoding them.
5	Nothing under `cheapy/routing/` or `cheapy/capability/` imports it, which keeps those
6	stages pure functions of their arguments and keeps the tests free of a config file.
7	
8	Precedence, resolved by `SimulationConfig.resolve()`:
9	
10	    command-line flag  >  cheapy.yaml  >  the DEFAULT_* constants below
11	
12	`cheapy.yaml` lives at the repo root and uses SHOUTING keys (`W_COST`, `BETA`, ...) to
13	match the names the report and the CLI help use. A missing file is not an error — the
14	built-in defaults are the shipped operating point.
15	"""
16	
17	from __future__ import annotations
18	
19	from dataclasses import dataclass, fields
20	from pathlib import Path
21	from typing import Any
22	
23	REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
24	CONFIG_NAME = "cheapy.yaml"
25	DEFAULT_CONFIG_PATH = REPO_ROOT / CONFIG_NAME
26	
27	#: Equal weighting: the midpoint of the cost/quality frontier, not a tuned optimum.
28	DEFAULT_W_COST = 0.5
29	DEFAULT_W_PERFORMANCE = 0.5
30	
31	#: Conformity weighting of the capability model (`w_i = prior_i ** BETA`). Mirrors
32	#: `cheapy.capability.capability_model.DEFAULT_BETA`; kept as a literal so a missing
33	#: config file never depends on import order between the two modules.
34	DEFAULT_BETA = 3.0
35	
36	#: Optimistic prefix-cache bound — see `cheapy/preprocessing/trajectory_analyzer.py`.
37	DEFAULT_CACHE_HIT_RATE = 1.0
38	
39	DEFAULT_VERBOSE = False
40	
41	#: config key -> field name. The YAML keys are the public names; the dataclass fields are
42	#: exactly the keyword arguments the router and the analyzer take.
43	_KEYS = {
44	    "W_COST": "w_cost",
45	    "W_PERFORMANCE": "w_performance",
46	    "BETA": "beta",
47	    "CACHE_HIT_RATE": "cache_hit_rate",
48	    "VERBOSE": "verbose",
49	}
50	
51	__all__ = ["SimulationConfig", "load_config", "CONFIG_NAME", "DEFAULT_CONFIG_PATH"]
52	
53	
54	@dataclass(frozen=True)
55	class SimulationConfig:
56	    """One resolved set of simulation settings."""
57	
58	    w_cost: float = DEFAULT_W_COST
59	    w_performance: float = DEFAULT_W_PERFORMANCE
60	    beta: float = DEFAULT_BETA
61	    cache_hit_rate: float = DEFAULT_CACHE_HIT_RATE
62	    verbose: bool = DEFAULT_VERBOSE
63	
64	    def resolve(self, **overrides: Any) -> SimulationConfig:
65	        """Return a copy with every non-`None` override applied.
66	
67	        `None` means "the flag was not given", which is why the CLI's argparse defaults
68	        are all `None` rather than the numbers — otherwise a default would silently
69	        outrank the config file.
70	        """
71	        known = {f.name for f in fields(self)}
72	        unknown = set(overrides) - known
73	        if unknown:
74	            raise TypeError(f"unknown setting(s): {', '.join(sorted(unknown))}")
75	        merged = {f.name: getattr(self, f.name) for f in fields(self)}
76	        merged.update({k: v for k, v in overrides.items() if v is not None})
77	        return SimulationConfig(**merged)
78	
79	    def validate(self) -> SimulationConfig:
80	        """Reject values the scoring stages cannot interpret, at the boundary."""
81	        if self.w_cost < 0 or self.w_performance < 0:
82	            raise ValueError("W_COST and W_PERFORMANCE must be >= 0")
83	        if self.w_cost + self.w_performance <= 0:
84	            raise ValueError("W_COST + W_PERFORMANCE must be > 0 (they are normalized by their sum)")
85	        if self.beta < 0:
86	            raise ValueError(f"BETA must be >= 0, got {self.beta}")
87	        if not 0.0 <= self.cache_hit_rate <= 1.0:
88	            raise ValueError(f"CACHE_HIT_RATE must be in [0, 1], got {self.cache_hit_rate}")
89	        return self
90	
91	
92	def _coerce(key: str, value: Any) -> Any:
93	    """YAML gives us the right types already; this only guards hand-edited strings."""
94	    if key == "VERBOSE":
95	        if isinstance(value, bool):
96	            return value
97	        if isinstance(value, str):
98	            return value.strip().lower() in {"1", "true", "yes", "on"}
99	        return bool(value)
100	    try:
101	        return float(value)
102	    except (TypeError, ValueError) as exc:
103	        raise ValueError(f"{key} in {CONFIG_NAME} must be a number, got {value!r}") from exc
104	
105	
106	def load_config(path: Path | str | None = None) -> SimulationConfig:
107	    """Read `cheapy.yaml` (or `path`) into a `SimulationConfig`.
108	
109	    A missing default config falls back to the built-in defaults; a missing *explicit*
110	    path is an error, because asking for a file that is not there is a typo, not a
111	    choice. Unknown keys are an error too — a silently ignored `W_PRICE:` would look
112	    like the router disregarding your settings.
113	    """
114	    explicit = path is not None
115	    config_path = Path(path) if explicit else DEFAULT_CONFIG_PATH
116	
117	    if not config_path.exists():
118	        if explicit:
119	            raise FileNotFoundError(f"config file not found: {config_path}")
120	        return SimulationConfig()
121	
122	    import yaml  # local import: only the CLI path needs PyYAML installed
123	
124	    raw = yaml.safe_load(config_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")) or {}
125	    if not isinstance(raw, dict):
126	        raise ValueError(f"{config_path} must be a mapping of KEY: value")
127	
128	    unknown = set(raw) - set(_KEYS)
129	    if unknown:
130	        raise ValueError(
131	            f"unknown key(s) in {config_path}: {', '.join(sorted(unknown))}. "
132	            f"Known keys: {', '.join(_KEYS)}"

1	"""Assign `price_score` to each candidate `ModelLLM` for one `Trajectory`.
2	
3	Per the README's scoring contract (§5): `price_score` is `[0, 1]`, higher = cheaper,
4	normalized *within this trajectory's candidate pool* — not against some global price
5	scale. This module is a pure function of `(Trajectory, List[ModelLLM])`; the only place
6	it reads `Trajectory.served_model` is the switching-cost check below, which the README
7	explicitly carves out as legitimate (it is not a task-quality proxy).
8	
9	The crux, per docs/FULL_REPORT.md §5: providers cache the shared input prefix across a trajectory's
10	calls, and a model switch resets that cache. So "cheaper per token" and "cheaper for
11	the next call" are different questions once a trajectory has accumulated context — a
12	model switch pays full uncached price for the whole next prompt, which in long
13	trajectories can dwarf any per-token saving. That's the entire reason this module needs
14	`served_model` at all: to tell a HOLD's mostly-cached next call apart from a CHANGE's
15	fully-uncached one.
16	
17	The base for "how big is the next prompt" is `Trajectory.last_call_input_tokens`, not
18	`total_tokens` -- see `_next_call_tokens` for why: every call resends the whole history
19	up to that point, so the next call's size tracks the size of the *most recent* call, not
20	the sum of every past call's own (already-superseded) full-history snapshot.
21	"""
22	
23	from __future__ import annotations
24	
25	from cheapy.models.llm import ModelLLM
26	from cheapy.models.trajectory import Trajectory
27	
28	
29	def _next_call_tokens(trajectory: Trajectory) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
30	    """ESTIMATE the shape of the trajectory's next call.
31	
32	    Returns (last_call_input_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens).
33	
34	    `last_call_input_tokens` is `Trajectory.last_call_input_tokens` taken at face value:
35	    the size of the most recently recovered call's full prompt (tool schemas + history
36	    up to that point). Because every call resends the whole history, this is the best
37	    available proxy for the size of the *next* call's prompt.
38	
39	    This deliberately does NOT use `total_tokens`. `total_tokens` sums every past call's
40	    prompt -- each of which was itself a full-history resend at the time -- so it adds up
41	    several superseded snapshots of a growing thing instead of reporting the size of the
42	    latest one. On a trajectory whose prompt grows roughly linearly over `n` calls,
43	    `total_tokens` overstates the real next-call size by very roughly a factor of `n/2`,
44	    and can trip the context-window feasibility gate below for a model that would
45	    actually serve the real next call fine. `last_call_input_tokens` doesn't have that
46	    problem: it's one call's real size, not an accumulating sum.
47	
48	    `increment_tokens` approximates how much *new* content (tool outputs, replies, ...)
49	    a typical call in this trajectory appends, as the trajectory's own average per-call
50	    growth (`last_call_input_tokens / total_calls`) -- not `total_tokens / total_calls`,
51	    which is the same superseded-snapshots mistake `last_call_input_tokens` exists to
52	    avoid, just applied to the increment instead of the prompt size: it averages in
53	    every past call's own (smaller, since-outgrown) prompt size, not how much this
54	    trajectory actually grows per step. There is no better signal available for the
55	    increment itself: the next call's actual new content is by definition not in the
56	    log yet. This average is a separate, smaller known simplification (it can over- or
57	    under-estimate a single step depending on whether the trajectory's growth is
58	    front- or back-loaded) -- see the README's "Known simplifications".
59	    """
60	    last_call_input_tokens = float(trajectory.last_call_input_tokens)
61	    increment_tokens = (
62	        last_call_input_tokens / trajectory.total_calls if trajectory.total_calls else 0.0
63	    )
64	    next_output_tokens = trajectory.avg_output_tokens_per_call
65	    return last_call_input_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens
66	
67	
68	def _next_call_cost(trajectory: Trajectory, model: ModelLLM) -> float:
69	    """ESTIMATE the USD cost of `model` serving this trajectory's next call.
70	
71	    No candidate is ever excluded for having too small a context window. If
72	    `last_call_input_tokens` is bigger than what `model` can hold, this assumes the
73	    context gets compacted down to the model's max `context_window_size` before the
74	    call is sent -- clamp the size, then price it with the exact same cache-aware
75	    formula used for every other call, holding or switching alike.
76	    """
77	    last_call_input_tokens, increment_tokens, next_output_tokens = _next_call_tokens(
78	        trajectory
79	    )
80	    last_call_input_tokens = min(last_call_input_tokens, float(model.context_window_size))
81	    next_input_tokens = last_call_input_tokens + increment_tokens
82	
83	    holding = model.name == trajectory.served_model
84	    if holding:
85	        # Same model as the log: the last call's whole prompt was already sent once and
86	        # is cache-eligible; only the new increment is guaranteed uncached. Cap at
87	        # `last_call_input_tokens` -- `total_cached_tokens` is a whole-trajectory
88	        # aggregate and can exceed the size of any single call, but only that much of it
89	        # is actually part of *this* call's bill.
90	        cached_tokens = min(float(trajectory.total_cached_tokens), last_call_input_tokens)
91	        uncached_tokens = (last_call_input_tokens - cached_tokens) + increment_tokens
92	    else:
93	        # A switch resets the provider's prefix cache: the whole next prompt is
94	        # uncached, not just the increment. This is the cache trap from docs/FULL_REPORT.md §5.
95	        cached_tokens = 0.0
96	        uncached_tokens = next_input_tokens
97	
98	    input_cost = (
99	        uncached_tokens * model.input_price_per_1m
100	        + cached_tokens * model.cached_input_price_per_1m
101	    ) / 1_000_000
102	    output_cost = next_output_tokens * model.output_price_per_1m / 1_000_000
103	    return input_cost + output_cost
104	
105	
106	def estimate_costs(trajectory: Trajectory, models: list[ModelLLM]) -> dict[str, float]:
107	    """ESTIMATE the USD cost of each candidate in `models` serving the trajectory's next
108	    call, keyed by model name — see `_next_call_cost`.
109	
110	    Public so callers other than `score_price` -- e.g. a benchmark comparing policies by
111	    actual dollar cost rather than the normalized `price_score` -- can get the same
112	    per-candidate cost figures `score_price` normalizes, without duplicating the
113	    cache-trap cost logic in `_next_call_cost`.
114	    """
115	    return {model.name: _next_call_cost(trajectory, model) for model in models}
116	
117	
118	def score_price(trajectory: Trajectory, models: list[ModelLLM]) -> list[ModelLLM]:
119	    """Enrich each `ModelLLM` in `models` with a `price_score` in `(0, 1]`.
120	
121	    Higher is cheaper. Costs are estimated per `_next_call_cost` (via `estimate_costs`)
122	    and scored as a ratio to the *cheapest* candidate in this trajectory's candidate
123	    pool — per docs/FULL_REPORT.md §5's "normalize within the candidate pool, not globally" — rather
124	    than min-max stretched across the pool's full price range. A candidate priced at `k`
125	    times the cheapest one scores `1/k`: a candidate only marginally above the cheapest
126	    price lands close to `1.0`, not at the same `0.0` floor a wildly pricier candidate
127	    would get under min-max. It also depends only on the cheapest cost, not the
128	    priciest, so a candidate's score no longer shifts just because some unrelated,
129	    pricier (or cheaper) candidate joins the pool. Every candidate gets a real cost (a
130	    too-small context window is compacted to fit, never excluded — see
131	    `_next_call_cost`), so every model in the pool gets a ratio-based score.
132	    """
133	    costs = estimate_costs(trajectory, models)
134	    cheapest = min(costs.values())
135	
136	    for model in models:
137	        cost = costs[model.name]
138	        # cost == 0 only when cheapest == 0 too (costs are never negative), so this is
139	        # the tie-at-the-top case, not a magic number -- 0/0 is otherwise undefined.
140	        model.price_score = 1.0 if cost == 0 else cheapest / cost
141	
142	    return models

#: way `performance_model.DEFAULT_BETA` was: measured, not asserted -- see
#: `research/legacy/price_exponent_sweep.py` and docs/FULL_REPORT.md §5/§7 for the sweep
#: this value came out of.
DEFAULT_PRICE_EXPONENT = 0.25


def score_price(
    trajectory: Trajectory, models: list[ModelLLM], price_exponent: float = DEFAULT_PRICE_EXPONENT
) -> list[ModelLLM]:
    """Enrich each `ModelLLM` in `models` with a `price_score` in `(0, 1]`.

    Higher is cheaper. Costs are estimated per `_next_call_cost` (via `estimate_costs`)
    and scored as a ratio to the *cheapest* candidate in this trajectory's candidate
    pool — per docs/FULL_REPORT.md §5's "normalize within the candidate pool, not globally" — rather
    than min-max stretched across the pool's full price range. A candidate priced at `k`
    times the cheapest one scores `(1/k) ** price_exponent`: a candidate only marginally
    above the cheapest price lands close to `1.0`, not at the same `0.0` floor a wildly
    pricier candidate would get under min-max. It also depends only on the cheapest
    cost, not the priciest, so a candidate's score no longer shifts just because some
    unrelated, pricier (or cheaper) candidate joins the pool. Every candidate gets a
    real cost (a too-small context window is compacted to fit, never excluded — see
    `_next_call_cost`), so every model in the pool gets a ratio-based score.

    `price_exponent` compresses that ratio's dynamic range before it is used.
    `price_score`'s raw ratio-to-cheapest can span the pool's full price spread (this
    project's 9 candidates: 1.0 down to 0.02, a 50x range), while `performance_score`
    is designed to compress toward the top whenever candidates broadly agree (docs/FULL_REPORT.md
    §6) -- nothing below ~0.80 on settled steps, ~0.17 spread even on contested ones. In
    a linear weighted average, whichever score has the wider numeric spread dominates
    almost regardless of the weight given to it (docs/FULL_REPORT.md §7's "price saturates at
    w_cost = 0.15"). Raising the ratio to `price_exponent < 1` pulls every sub-1.0 score
    up toward `1.0` -- the cheapest candidate is unaffected (`1.0 ** p == 1.0` for any
    `p`) -- narrowing price_score's spread to roughly the same order of magnitude as
    performance_score's, so the weight actually trades the two off across more of its
    range instead of one term swamping the other by construction. `price_exponent = 1.0`
    reproduces the plain ratio; this is a strict generalization, not a different formula.
    """
    costs = estimate_costs(trajectory, models)
    cheapest = min(costs.values())

    for model in models:
        cost = costs[model.name]
        # cost == 0 only when cheapest == 0 too (costs are never negative), so this is
        # the tie-at-the-top case, not a magic number -- 0/0 is otherwise undefined, and
        # 1.0 to any power is still 1.0 so price_exponent doesn't need special-casing here.
        model.price_score = 1.0 if cost == 0 else (cheapest / cost) ** price_exponent

    return models

    """Exercises the `price_exponent` compression itself."""

    def test_exponent_one_reproduces_the_plain_ratio(self):

            served_model="model-a",

        self.assertAlmostEqual(compressed, 0.55**0.25)
        self.assertGreater(compressed, raw)

    def test_cheapest_candidate_is_unaffected_by_the_exponent(self):
        # 1.0 ** p == 1.0 for any p: the cheapest candidate's score doesn't move,
        # whatever compression is applied.
        trajectory = make_trajectory(
            served_model="model-a",
            total_calls=5,
            last_call_input_tokens=3_000,
            total_cached_tokens=1_800,
        )
        for p in (1.0, 0.5, 0.25, 0.05):
            models = [make_model("model-a"), make_model("model-b")]
            score_price(trajectory, models, price_exponent=p)
            self.assertEqual(models[0].price_score, 1.0)

    def test_default_exponent_narrows_the_pools_full_price_spread(self):
        # The whole point: a 50x-pricier candidate should no longer score anywhere near
        # min-max's 0.0, nor even the plain ratio's 0.02 -- it should land within a much
        # narrower band of the cheapest candidate's 1.0, comparable in order of
        # magnitude to performance_score's typical spread.
        trajectory = make_trajectory(
            served_model="model-a",
            total_calls=5,
            last_call_input_tokens=3_000,
            total_cached_tokens=1_800,
        )
        cheap = make_model("cheap", input_price_per_1m=0.2, cached_input_price_per_1m=0.02)
        pricey = make_model(
            "pricey", input_price_per_1m=10.0, cached_input_price_per_1m=1.0
        )  # 50x cheap's rate
        models = [cheap, pricey]

        score_price(trajectory, models, price_exponent=DEFAULT_PRICE_EXPONENT)

        by_name = {m.name: m.price_score for m in models}
        self.assertEqual(by_name["cheap"], 1.0)
        self.assertGreater(by_name["pricey"], 0.3)  # nowhere near the raw ratio's ~0.02

315	  switching cost. Leaking the served model into a score is how you accidentally build a classifier
316	  that predicts the log instead of a router that improves on it.
317	
318	### Price
319	
320	**Token counts are estimates.** There is no `usage` field. The pipeline counts with **`tiktoken`,
321	`o200k_base`, applied uniformly to every line of both families** (`trajectory_analyzer.count_tokens`);

323	degrades instead of failing. Every derived number is an estimate and must be labeled as one.
324

326	  Claude text by 4% and GPT text by 9% — a 5-point **family-correlated** error, because tool-call

328	  tool-heavy. On a workload this tool-dominated it is wrong exactly where it matters.
329	- *Why one tokenizer for both:* the ids are anonymized and map to no public tokenizer
330	  (`encoding_for_model("claude-opus-5")` raises), and Claude's tokenizer is not available offline.
331	  A per-family tokenizer would make the two families' prices incomparable — the only comparison the
332	  router makes. Uniform is the honest choice; it is still an estimate.
333	- Cost: ~16 s for the full export, offline after a one-time 3.6 MB vocab fetch cached in
334	  `.tokenizer_cache/` (gitignored).

337	— and they sit at the very front of the prefix, so they are also the most cacheable part.
338	`total_tokens` includes them.
339	
340	**Pricing is an assumption.** The ids are anonymized, so no public price sheet applies. The
341	assumed sheet lives in one place, `src/cheapy/preprocessing/model_list.py`, so it can be swapped wholesale

343	placeholder; neither pricing source discounts a freshly generated output token.
344

346	trajectory's calls. A model switch **resets that cache**, so every call after a switch pays full
347	price for the entire accumulated prefix. In trajectories this long that penalty can dwarf the
348	per-token saving that motivated the switch. A `CHANGE TO` that ignores this looks brilliant and is

356	  prefix-extension of call *i−1*'s, so under a perfect cache the cached share of call *i* is

1	# Cheapy — Viktor Challenge submission
2	
3	**Members:** Pietro Quinzani · João Sandre · Rodrigo Takahashi
4	
5	Viktor pins one model for a whole trajectory. Cheapy reads the trace and picks which of nine
6	models should serve the *next* call — `HOLD`, or `CHANGE TO <model>` — from a price score and a
7	capability score. Offline, no API keys.
8	
9	**Objective:** cost per call vs. capability retained. Cost is *quadratic* in trajectory length —
10	every call re-sends the whole history, and 92% of billed input in the export is re-sent prefix. So
11	the money is in long trajectories, and the question is: which is the cheapest model still able to
12	take this step? We optimize the **frontier**, not a point: `W_COST` / `W_PERFORMANCE` in
13	[`cheapy.yaml`](cheapy.yaml) dial from "cheapest acceptable" to "best regardless of cost".
14	
15	**Routing signal:** prefix-cache structure and step shape. Call `i`'s prompt is by construction a
16	prefix-extension of call `i−1`'s, so the cached share is exact rather than searched for, and a
17	switch resets that cache — the price score prices that directly. The capability score reads the
18	step only: prefix size, call count, tool-calls per call, distinct-tool ratio, repeated-tool runs,
19	recent error rate, last output length, token shares, toolset size, Slack vs Teams, subagent flag.
20	Model identity enters as a prior alone, so nothing is downstream of who actually served the call.
21	
22	**Headline result (cache-aware, all 1,000 trajectories, estimated tokens):** at `W_COST = 0.10`,
23	**−63.1% estimated next-call cost** vs. today's incumbent-only policy ($0.0277 → $0.0102 per
24	trajectory), keeping **98.4% of the incumbent's mean capability score**; at `W_COST ≥ 0.15` it
25	saturates at **−78.2%**. **That second number is the router's own proxy, not a measured outcome** —
26	the export has no outcome to hold out. Held-out numbers exist for the proxy itself:
27	leave-one-probe-out R² +0.007 / +0.027 / +0.035, positive in all three folds.
28	
29	**Off-policy method:** elicitation + pairwise conformity — a judge panel, not matching or
30	weighting. We cut 957 trajectories at a random step, asked three probes what action they would
31	take, scored agreement against the logged action, fit a pairwise-agreement regressor on the
32	features above, and Nyström-completed the 15 pairs we could never query (OpenAI credits only).
33	**Weakest point: the capability signal is far weaker than price, so the router collapses into
34	"always the cheapest model".** R² = 1.4%; capability separates candidates by ~0.17, price by orders
35	of magnitude. The crossover band is `W_COST` ≈ 0.05–0.08; above it, ~98% of trajectories go to one
36	model. Two things we don't paper over: 98% *mean* retention hides that only **37.5%** of individual
37	trajectories keep a pick at-or-above their incumbent, and agreement isn't quality — the noise floor
38	is 0.86, which is how often a probe agrees with *itself*.

EXPORT = Path("export/trajectories_v1_01.jsonl")
PRICE_EXPONENT = 0.25
BETA = 3.0
W_COST_GRID = [0.00, 0.02, 0.05, 0.08, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25, 0.50, 1.00]


def main() -> None:
    base_models = build_model_list()
    trajectories = list(analyze_file(EXPORT))
    n = len(trajectories)
    print(f"loaded {n} trajectories\n")

    # Precompute price_score/performance_score once per trajectory (independent of
    # w_cost), reuse across the whole grid -- only aggregate_scores/decide change.
    scored: list[tuple] = []
    incumbent_costs = []
    for traj in trajectories:
        models: list[ModelLLM] = [m.model_copy(deep=True) for m in base_models]
        score_price(traj, models, price_exponent=PRICE_EXPONENT)
        score_performance(traj, models, beta=BETA)
        costs = estimate_costs(traj, models)
        incumbent_costs.append(costs[traj.served_model])
        scored.append((traj, models, costs))

    incumbent_cost_avg = sum(incumbent_costs) / n
    print(f"incumbent-only avg cost: ${incumbent_cost_avg:.6f}/trajectory\n")

    header = f"{'w_cost':>7} {'HOLD':>12} {'cost_vs_incumbent':>18} {'capability_kept':>16}  changes_go_to"
    print(header)
    print("-" * len(header))

    for w_cost in W_COST_GRID:
        w_perf = round(1 - w_cost, 2)
        hold = 0
        router_costs = []
        picked_perf = []
        incumbent_perf = []
        targets: Counter[str] = Counter()

        for traj, models, costs in scored:
            # aggregate_scores mutates final_score in place -- re-run per w_cost on a
            # copy-free pass since price_score/performance_score are untouched.
            aggregate_scores(models, w_cost=w_cost, w_performance=w_perf)
            d = decide(traj, models, min_gain=0.0)
            if d.action == "HOLD":
                hold += 1
            else:
                targets[d.top_model] += 1
            router_costs.append(costs[d.top_model])
            picked_perf.append(d.top_performance_score)
            served_model = next((m for m in models if m.name == traj.served_model), None)
            incumbent_perf.append(served_model.performance_score if served_model else None)

        router_cost_avg = sum(router_costs) / n
        cost_vs_incumbent = 100 * (router_cost_avg / incumbent_cost_avg - 1)

        valid_pairs = [
            (p, i) for p, i in zip(picked_perf, incumbent_perf) if p is not None and i is not None
        ]
        picked_mean = sum(p for p, _ in valid_pairs) / len(valid_pairs)
        incumbent_mean = sum(i for _, i in valid_pairs) / len(valid_pairs)
        capability_kept = 100 * picked_mean / incumbent_mean

        top_targets = ", ".join(f"{name} {count}" for name, count in targets.most_common(3))
        print(
            f"{w_cost:>7.2f} {hold:>5} ({100*hold/n:>5.1f}%) {cost_vs_incumbent:>+17.1f}% "
            f"{capability_kept:>15.1f}%  {top_targets}"
        )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

#### The formula (`src/cheapy/routing/price_model.py`)

`score_price(trajectory, models, price_exponent=DEFAULT_PRICE_EXPONENT)` estimates the USD cost of
each candidate serving the trajectory's **next call**, then scores each cost as a *ratio to the
cheapest candidate* in the pool for this trajectory, raised to `price_exponent`:
`price_score = (cheapest_cost / cost) ** price_exponent ∈ (0, 1]`, cheapest → `1.0` for any
exponent (`1.0 ** p == 1.0`), and a candidate priced at `k` times the cheapest one → `(1/k) **
price_exponent`. This is deliberately not min-max normalization (`(max_cost − cost) / (max_cost −
min_cost)`): min-max forces the priciest candidate to exactly `0.0` and the cheapest to exactly
`1.0` regardless of how close their actual costs are, so a candidate only 1% pricier than the
cheapest gets the same `0.0` floor as one 100× pricier, and every candidate's score shifts whenever
an unrelated candidate's price changes the pool's max. Ratio-to-cheapest scores each candidate from
its own cost and the pool's cheapest cost only, so a marginally pricier candidate gets a
proportionally mild penalty and an unrelated candidate joining the pool doesn't move anyone else's
score. It reads only `Trajectory` fields plus one `ModelLLM` at a time — the only place it looks at
`trajectory.served_model` is the hold/switch cache check below, which is the exception the shared
contract above carves out.

**Why `price_exponent` exists.** The plain ratio (`price_exponent = 1.0`) still spans the pool's
full price spread — this project's 9 candidates: `1.0` down to `~0.02`, a 50× range — while
`performance_score` is designed to compress toward the top whenever candidates broadly agree (§6):
nothing below `~0.80` on settled steps, `~0.17` spread even on contested ones. In the linear
weighted average (§5, "Aggregation"), whichever score has the wider numeric spread dominates almost
regardless of the weight it's given — this is the mechanism behind "price saturates" below.
`price_exponent < 1.0` raises every sub-`1.0` ratio toward `1.0` (the cheapest candidate is
unaffected, `1.0 ** p == 1.0` for any `p`), narrowing price_score's spread to roughly the same order
of magnitude as performance_score's, so the weight actually trades the two off across more of its
range instead of one term swamping the other by construction. `price_exponent = 1.0` reproduces the
plain ratio exactly — this is a strict generalization of the formula, not a different one.
`DEFAULT_PRICE_EXPONENT = 0.25`, set by comparing it against `0.20` and `0.30` on the full export at
`W_COST = 0.1` (§7) — **not yet a proper grid sweep the way `BETA` was justified (§6)**; treat it as
a working default, not a tuned optimum (§10, open decisions).

1	# Cheapy — Viktor Challenge submission
2	
3	**Members:** Pietro Quinzani · João Sandre · Rodrigo Takahashi
4	
5	Viktor pins one model for a whole trajectory. Cheapy reads the trace and picks which of nine
6	models should serve the *next* call — `HOLD`, or `CHANGE TO <model>` — from a price score and a
7	capability score. Offline, no API keys.
8	
9	**Objective:** cost per call vs. capability retained. Cost is *quadratic* in trajectory length —
10	every call re-sends the whole history, and 92% of billed input in the export is re-sent prefix. So
11	the money is in long trajectories, and the question is: which is the cheapest model still able to
12	take this step? We optimize the **frontier**, not a point: `W_COST` / `W_PERFORMANCE` in
13	[`cheapy.yaml`](cheapy.yaml) dial from "cheapest acceptable" to "best regardless of cost".
14	
15	**Routing signal:** prefix-cache structure and step shape. Call `i`'s prompt is by construction a
16	prefix-extension of call `i−1`'s, so the cached share is exact rather than searched for, and a
17	switch resets that cache — the price score prices that directly. The capability score reads the
18	step only: prefix size, call count, tool-calls per call, distinct-tool ratio, repeated-tool runs,
19	recent error rate, last output length, token shares, toolset size, Slack vs Teams, subagent flag.
20	Model identity enters as a prior alone, so nothing is downstream of who actually served the call.
21

23	**−63.1% estimated next-call cost** vs. today's incumbent-only policy ($0.0277 → $0.0102 per
24	trajectory), keeping **98.4% of the incumbent's mean capability score**; at `W_COST ≥ 0.15` it
25	saturates at **−78.2%**. **That second number is the router's own proxy, not a measured outcome** —
26	the export has no outcome to hold out. Held-out numbers exist for the proxy itself:
27	leave-one-probe-out R² +0.007 / +0.027 / +0.035, positive in all three folds.
28	
29	**Off-policy method:** elicitation + pairwise conformity — a judge panel, not matching or
30	weighting. We cut 957 trajectories at a random step, asked three probes what action they would
31	take, scored agreement against the logged action, fit a pairwise-agreement regressor on the
32	features above, and Nyström-completed the 15 pairs we could never query (OpenAI credits only).

800	weighting across comparable trajectories, judge-model rescoring of individual calls. Cheapy's
801	answer is the third of those: a three-model judge panel, elicited offline, reduced to a pairwise
802	agreement model (§6).
803	
804	**What §7's two axes are actually worth.** The cost axis is a deterministic formula over estimated
805	tokens — no fitting, no counterfactual, so "−63.1%" is as good as the token estimate and the
806	`CACHE_HIT_RATE` assumption behind it, and no better. The quality axis is *not* a realized
807	outcome: it is the mean `performance_score` of the pick, i.e. predicted agreement with a panel of
808	three probes, whose own held-out R² is +0.007 to +0.035 and whose measurement noise floor is 0.86.
809	Calling it "98% of quality kept" would overstate what was measured; "98% of the proxy the router
810	itself optimizes" is what the number says. Closing that gap — realized quality on held-out
811	trajectories — is the open work.
812	
813	Naming where the estimate can fail is **scored, not penalized**. The deliverable is a frontier, not
814	a point, and a five-minute presentation with one chart, one claim, and one known weakness.
